Self-improvement

What it is?

Let’s define self-improvement. The definition of self-improvement is pretty self-explanatory: Self-improvement is the improvement of one’s knowledge, status, or character by one’s own efforts. It’s the quest to make ourselves better in any and every facet of life.

Key Areas

  1. Personal Development

    • Emotional Intelligence
    • Self-Awareness
    • Confidence
    • Motivation

  2. Skills Development

    • Communication Skills
    • Time Management
    • Leadership Skills
    • Problem-Solving Skills

  3. Health and Well-being

    • Physical Fitness
    • Mental Health
    • Healthy Eating
    • Stress Management

  4. Career Advancement

    • Networking
    • Professional Skills
    • Goal Setting
    • Continuous Learning

Important aspects

  1. Goal Setting

    • Define clear, achievable goals
    • Use SMART criteria (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)

  2. Continuous Learning

    • Read books, take courses, attend workshops
    • Stay updated with industry trends

  3. Self-Reflection

    • Regularly assess your progress
    • Identify strengths and areas for improvement

  4. Habits Formation

    • Develop positive daily routines
    • Use techniques like habit stacking

  5. Mindfulness and Meditation

    • Practice mindfulness to stay present
    • Use meditation to reduce stress and increase focus

  6. Seeking Feedback

    • Ask for constructive criticism
    • Learn from mentors and peers

  7. Time Management

    • Prioritize tasks effectively
    • Use tools like planners and apps

  8. Networking and Relationships

    • Build strong personal and professional relationships
    • Engage in active listening and empathy

Personal development skills

Personal development skills are qualities and abilities that help you grow both personally and professionally. In other words, they are skills that help you nurture your personal development. Understanding and improving these skills is a process also known as self-development or personal growth.


Importance

Personal development skills are important because they allow you to create strategic and tactical plans for personal and professional growth toward your goals. It can be helpful to hone personal development skills so you can naturally work them into your daily routines and use them to:

  • Achieve personal and career goals
  • Advance in your career
  • Improve your strengths and talents
  • Better yourself
  • Find fulfillment and satisfaction


How to improve

Face your fears

Fear hinders growth and progress. Overcome public speaking fears with classes or groups, tackle risk aversion by finding a mentor for guidance and confidence, and push past shyness by initiating conversations at events.

Read

Reading can expand your knowledge and vocabulary and keep you informed. It can also stimulate your mind and can improve your critical thinking skills. Try reading at least one educational or motivational article a day or book a month.

Learn something new

Learn a new skill or topic independently or through classes, like a new language, software, creative writing, or attend webinars on entrepreneurship or social media marketing.

Be open to feedback

Approach a family member, friend, colleague or manager, and ask them to give you feedback on a recent project or accomplishment. Use their positive comments as well as their constructive criticism to find ways to improve. Sometimes you need an outside, unbiased opinion to get a different perspective.

Network

By interacting with many people, you can learn new ideas and understand how to communicate and work with different personality types. You can also meet people and develop relationships that might help you in the future. Network through industry organizations and shared interest groups, or attend conferences and events on topics that interest you.

Keep a journal

Writing in a journal every day or week can help you gain self-awareness and reflect on recent events, decisions and conversations. You might keep a hand-written, private journal or choose to share your thoughts and experiences by blogging. Use it to set and assess goals and progress.

Find a mentor

Talk to a mentor if you need help identifying ways to build your self-development skills. This individual could be a manager, professor, someone you admire or a professional personal growth mentor.

Skillset

Goal setting

On your journey toward your best self, you need to set goals. The key is balance: If your goals are too lofty, you’ll get discouraged when you fall short. Start too small, and you’ll become satisfied with your progress too early and stop pushing yourself forward.


The better approach is to think in milestones. If you want to be a novelist, don’t set a goal to finish a book in a week. Focus on getting a couple of pages done each day, or on writing a chapter each week. This measurable progress is more sustainable and fulfilling.

Stress management

Personal growth can create a lot of stress.


“Growth and comfort do not coexist.” — Ginny Rometty, former CEO of IBM.


To keep going when times are tough, you have to learn how to manage your stress levels. If brisk walks help you keep your head on straight, schedule one for your lunch period every day. If you need to take Sundays off to recharge for the next week, it’s more than acceptable to do so.

Organization

Organization is a skill that comes more naturally to some people than others. If you’re a naturally messy person, start small. Otherwise, you’ll get overwhelmed.


Focus on the places where you spend the most time. Clean up your bedroom or vacuum your car. If physical cleaning is stressful, start by culling files from your computer. Believe it or not, one clean space can set the tone for the rest of your life.

Problem solving

On the road of personal development, you’ll run into some barriers. Nobody but you can remove these from your path. That’s why problem solving is a vital skill for self-development.

Time management

To master yourself, you must master your time. You only get so much of it, and every minute wasted is a minute you’ll never get back. The good news is, time management is a skill that transcends every situation.

Work ethic

You can wish for something all you want. But if you’re not willing to put in the work, you won’t actually achieve it.


The first step is acknowledging the work you need to do for personal development. The second is actually getting your hands dirty.


If you want to squat a certain amount of weight, you have to spend hours in the gym. Simply imagining yourself becoming stronger will do nothing.

Accountability

You are responsible for your own actions. Hold yourself accountable to them. The sooner you do, the quicker you can get back on track after making a mistake.


If your personal development slows down because you opted to sleep in instead of getting up early to work out, don’t blame the cold, grey morning. You made that choice.

Networking

The fast track to self-development is through networking. By connecting with other professionals in your field, you gain access to the wisdom of those with more experience than you.


The internet makes networking incredibly easy. Social media sites like LinkedIn allow you to connect with workers and leaders from all corners of the globe. Make meaningful connections, and they’ll give you not just something to aspire to, but a helping hand along that path.

Empathy

The people around you impact your self-development more than you might realize. Treating them with empathy cracks the door not just to compassion and understanding, but to all sorts of mentorship opportunities.


Remember, mentorship is a two-way street. Mentors benefit just as much from the arrangement as mentees do. One study of CFOs who mentored others found the top benefit they cited was improving their own leadership skills.

Self-control

Self-development is no walk in the park. In challenging times, you’ll be tempted to find comfort in relaxing activities, such as playing video games or scrolling through social media. In order to truly progress, though, you have to learn self-control.


Smartphones in particular are a threat to self-control. The average person spends hours per day on their mobile devices. If you fall into that bucket, ask yourself: How could you use that time more productively?

Patience

“The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.” — An old Chinese proverb


Remember no meaningful goal is achieved overnight.

Be patient. Self-development is a process that can take years, even decades. Don’t beat yourself up if you don’t see immediate progress. Take pride and find joy in even your smallest accomplishments.

Resilience

When the going gets tough, the tough get going. In other words, you have to push yourself through hard situations. Every time you throw in the towel, you lose momentum that’s difficult to get back.


Resilience is a skill acquired through struggle. That may not sound encouraging when looking for quick self-development, but you’ll soon see the power that comes from never giving up.

Balance

Spend all your time at your profession, and you’ll become a master at your trade. Spend all your time with family, and you’ll have wonderful relationships — but fewer skills and a much smaller bank account.


The key to getting the best of all worlds is balance. If you’re tired of working on one thing, take a break. You can always come back later, when you’re feeling more up to it.

Self-care

Self-care means different things to different people, as it should. But the overarching truth holds for everyone: If you don’t care for your health, you won’t see the self-growth you want.


Make time to exercise regularly, either at home or at a local gym. Choose a diet that will supply you with the nutrients you need, and stay hydrated. Meditate at least once per day. And if you’re having trouble managing your health on your own, reach out to a professional.

Sacrifice

What do you have to give up to achieve your goals? When it comes to personal development, there’s always something.


When you’re learning a new skill — especially if you also work full-time — you can’t spend the night socializing with friends. You may even need to sacrifice your weekends.


While it’s important to find time to enjoy life, this isn’t the same as indulgence. Too much of any good thing is bad. Be prepared to give up a few pleasures in service to your self-development.

Growth mindset

A fixed mindset avoids challenges due to fear of failure, prioritizing appearances over learning, which hinders growth. In contrast, a growth mindset embraces challenges, values learning, and believes skills are honed through effort, leading to greater resilience and quality of life. Professionally, it drives continuous improvement and innovation, fostering collaborative and motivated teams. Career-wise, a growth mindset encourages seeking new opportunities and embracing failures as lessons, essential for advancement.

Distancing

One of the most liberating and important steps in any self-development journey involves letting go of the things in your life that you can’t control, so you have more time and energy to put into the things that you can. Letting go of what you can’t control can also help you to start living in the here and now, which is the only time we have any power.

Self-awareness

An integral part of personal growth involves practising self-awareness and reflection, so you can learn more about your strengths, weaknesses, reactions, habits, likes, dislikes, motivations, fears, and so on.


Self-awareness can help you better understand how to meet your own needs and how your actions can impact the world around you. Building self-awareness often means making a conscious effort to take stock of your reactions and behaviours to better understand how this could be affecting yourself and others – or how other people’s actions could be affecting you.

Creativity

Creativity, crucial for innovative solutions, stems from finding original ideas, making life enjoyable. Contrary to belief, creativity can be nurtured through games like Chess and Sudoku, solving puzzles, and expressive activities, thereby broadening thinking and fostering unique ideas.

Methods


Kaizen

What it is?

Kaizen (改善) is a Japanese philosophy meaning "change for the better" or "continuous improvement." Originating in the Japanese manufacturing sector (most famously the Toyota Production System) after World War II, it was later adapted into a personal development framework. The core premise is simple:

Small, incremental changes, applied consistently over time, lead to massive results.

The "1% Rule"

In mathematical terms, Kaizen is often described as becoming 1% better every day. While $1\%$ seems negligible, the power of compounding is staggering:

$$(1.01)^{365} = 37.78$$

By improving just 1% daily, you end up 37 times better by the end of a year.

Core principles

To apply Kaizen effectively, you need to shift your mindset from "Big Wins" to "Micro-Victories."

  • Standardize first, optimize later: You cannot improve a habit that doesn't exist. Establish a tiny baseline before trying to make it "perfect."
  • Discard conventional fixed ideas: Don't assume things "have to be this way." Question every inefficiency.
  • Don't seek perfection: Seek a 1% improvement. Perfectionism is the enemy of Kaizen because it causes procrastination.
  • Empowerment: In a personal context, this means taking extreme ownership of your environment to remove "friction."

"Three Pillars" of Kaizen

To understand Kaizen deeply, you must look past "self-help" and into its structural roots. It rests on three operational pillars:

1. Genba (The Real Place)

In management, Genba is the shop floor. In self-development, it is where your work actually happens.

  • The Concept: You cannot improve from an ivory tower. You must go to the "place of action" to see where time is being wasted.
  • Application: If you want to improve your focus, don't just "try harder." Sit at your desk and observe the physical and digital distractions that occur in real-time.

2. Muda (Elimination of Waste)

Kaizen isn't just about adding good habits; it’s about the surgical removal of Muda. There are 7 classic types of waste, which we can adapt to personal growth:

  • Over-processing: Doing more work than is required (perfectionism).
  • Waiting: Idle time between productive tasks.
  • Motion: Unnecessary movement (e.g., searching for files or tools).
  • Defects: Errors that require rework (e.g., poor communication).

3. Standardized Work

Kaizen is impossible without a "standard." If your process is chaotic, your results will be inconsistent. You must document your current "best way" of doing something, and only then can you improve it.

Advanced Kaizen Frameworks

The 5S Methodology (Visual Order)

Most people think this is just "cleaning," but in Kaizen, it's about reducing cognitive friction:

  1. Seiri (Sort): Remove everything from your environment that isn't essential.
  2. Seiton (Set in Order): A place for everything, and everything in its place (ergonomics of the mind).
  3. Seiso (Shine): Maintaining your tools and workspace daily.
  4. Seiketsu (Standardize): Creating the rules for the first three S's.
  5. Shitsuke (Sustain): The discipline to keep the cycle going.

The "5 Whys" (Root Cause Analysis)

When you fail or hit a plateau, Kaizen demands you find the root cause, not just treat the symptom.

  • Problem: "I didn't work out today."
  • 1. Why? I was too tired.
  • 2. Why? I didn't sleep well.
  • 3. Why? I was on my phone late at night.
  • 4. Why? I didn't have a "no-screens" rule.
  • 5. Why? (Root Cause): I haven't designed a nighttime wind-down routine.

The 10 Principles of Kaizen

  1. Abandon fixed ideas. (Stop saying "That’s just how I am.")
  2. Think of how to do it, not why it cannot be done.
  3. Do not make excuses. Deny the status quo.
  4. Do not seek perfection. A 60% improvement now is better than 100% later.
  5. Correct mistakes immediately.
  6. Do not spend money on Kaizen; use your wits.
  7. Wisdom is brought out when faced with hardship.
  8. Ask "Why?" five times to find the root cause.
  9. Seek the wisdom of ten people rather than the knowledge of one.
  10. Remember that Kaizen is endless.

Kaizen in Cognitive Science: The "Amygdala Bypass"

This is the "why" behind the "how." When we face a massive challenge, the amygdala (fear center) triggers a fight-or-flight response.

  • The "Big Goal" Trap: "I will build a $1M business" causes stress and paralysis.
  • The Kaizen Solution: By asking "What is the smallest possible step I can take to move forward?", you bypass the amygdala and engage the prefrontal cortex, where rational planning and creativity happen.

How to Apply Kaizen: The PDCA Cycle

The most effective way to implement Kaizen is through the PDCA Cycle (Plan-Do-Check-Act):

  1. Plan: Identify a small bottleneck. (e.g., "I want to read more, but I'm too tired at night.")
  2. Do: Implement the smallest possible change. (e.g., "Read exactly one page before bed.")
  3. Check: After a week, evaluate. Did you do it? Was it too hard?
  4. Act (Adjust): If it worked, keep it. If not, make the step even smaller (e.g., "Read one paragraph").

Kaizen vs. Innovation (Kaikaku)

It is helpful to understand where Kaizen fits compared to other types of change:

Feature

Kaizen (Continuous Improvement)

Kaikaku (Radical Innovation)

Effect

Long-term and undramatic.

Short-term and dramatic.

Pace

Small steps.

Giant leaps.

Risk

Low risk (easy to pivot).

High risk (expensive/exhausting).

Requirement

Daily discipline.

High energy/investment.

Focus

Process and details.

Results and transformation.

Strategic comparison

Feature

Kaizen

Kaikaku

Type

Evolutionary

Revolutionary

Scope

Small, localized changes

Entire system overhaul

Analogy

Tuning an engine while driving

Buying a new car

When to use?

Daily maintenance and growth

When the current system is fundamentally broken

How to actually "Live" Kaizen

  • Morning: Review your "Standard."
  • During Work: Identify one Muda (waste) and eliminate it.
  • Evening (The Hansei): Perform Hansei (self-reflection). Ask: "What did I do today that I can improve by 1% tomorrow?"


Focus on the 10%

What it is?

At its core, this concept is about extreme prioritization. It posits that in any given project, goal, or day, only 10% of your activities are truly transformative. The rest are either "maintenance" tasks or "noise."

Core philosophy

  • Depth over Breadth: Instead of being "a mile wide and an inch deep," you become an inch wide and a mile deep in the area that matters.
  • The Law of Diminishing Returns: Once you move past the most critical 10%, every additional hour spent yields less and less significant results.
  • Cognitive Load Management: By ignoring the 90%, you free up the mental energy required to achieve mastery in the 10%.

How to Identify Your 10%

To apply this, you must perform a "Brutal Audit" of your life or work. You can use the following formula to find your focus:

The Filtering Process

  1. List Everything: Write down every task or habit you currently perform.
  2. The "Impact vs. Effort" Matrix: Identify tasks that have the highest impact regardless of effort.
  3. The "Lead Domino" Question: Ask yourself: "If I could only do one thing today that would make everything else easier or unnecessary, what would it be?"

Practical Application: How to Use It

Applying the 10% Rule requires more than just identification; it requires protection of your time.

Step A: The Power Hour

Dedicate the first 90 minutes of your day exclusively to your 10%. Do not check emails, Slack, or social media. This is your "Deep Work" zone.

Step B: Ruthless Elimination/Delegation

For the remaining 90% of tasks:

  • Automate: Can a script or software do this?
  • Delegate: Can someone else do this 80% as well as I can?
  • Delete: What happens if I just stop doing this? (Often, the answer is "nothing.")

Step C: Iterative Refinement

Your 10% changes as you grow. Re-evaluate your focus every 30 days. What was your "critical 10%" last month might be "maintenance" this month.

Real-World Examples


Category

The 90% (The Noise)

The 10% (The Focus)

Fitness

Buying gear, tracking supplements, debating workout splits.

Consistent intensity & caloric/protein surplus or deficit.

Business

Tweaking website colors, organizing files, "networking" events.

Direct sales calls & product development.

Learning

Highlighting books, watching "how-to" videos, buying courses.

Active recall and practical application of 1 key concept.

Relationships

Small talk, social media comments, superficial outings.

Deep, uninterrupted quality time and active listening.

Why Most People Fail to Do This

  • The Fear of Missing Out (FOMO): People worry that by ignoring the 90%, they are losing opportunities. In reality, they are losing focus.
  • The Allure of "Fake Work": The 90% is usually easier and feels productive (e.g., clearing an inbox). The 10% is usually difficult, uncomfortable, and requires intense concentration.
  • Social Pressure: Society rewards "busyness." Choosing to do less (but better) often looks like laziness to the untrained eye.

Summary Table: The 10% Mindset


Feature

Traditional Productivity

The 10% Mindset

Goal

Get as much done as possible.

Get the right thing done perfectly.

Metric

Schedule

7 tips to wake up early

Have a strong "why"

If you don't come up with a good way to spend your mornings, they will automatically be allocated for sleeping in. Changing this habit is hard, and it you want to endure the difficulty, you will need a good reason for it.


Plan your morning

The more specific you are with your morning routine, the easier it's going to be to execute it. I'm talking about the really small details.


Put your alarm clock far from your bed

If it's right next to your bed, you will shut it off or hit snooze. Never hit snooze. If it's far from your bed, you have to get up out of bed to shut it off. By then, you're up. Now you just to have to stay up.


Don't make drastic changes.

Start slowly, by waking just 15-30 minutes earlier than causal. Get used to this for a few days. Then cut back another 15 minutes. Do this gradually until you get to your goal time.


Make waking up early a reward

Find something that's pleasurable to you and allow yourself to do it as part of your morning routine.


Take a cold shower

One tip that can help you wake up is to give yourself a blast of cold water for 30 seconds, switching to extremly hot for another 30 before going back to cold. Some people even forego the hot water completly and do a cold shower instead. Either way, if you injet cold into the shower routine, you're going to wake yourself up very effectively.


Challange yourself for 21 days

Waking up early for 1 or 2 days is easy. Being consistent about it and turning this into a habit is much better.


12 Things I Stole From People More Successful Than Me

Pare Down The Number of Decisions You Make Every Day

Simply put, every decision you make uses up your mental energy. So in order to save your mental power for the important decisions of the day, you have to learn to reduce the number of decisions you make on a daily basis either by automating them or delegating them.

By doing this, you’ll find yourself becoming significantly less stressed, more productive, and overall happier.


Tear Up Your To-Do List

Success is never achieved by the person who does the most things every day. Instead, success is always achieved by the person who does what is most important every day.

This is why to-do lists can oftentimes do more harm than good. Why? Because a to-do list is essentially everything you think you need to do, not everything you ought to do.


Turn “Have-To” Into “Get-To”

At one point in my life, I constantly struggled to build new habits. But here’s a simple idea that helped me overcome this: Don’t view your habits as challenges. Instead, view them as opportunities.


Use People’s Favorite Sound

Remembering and using someone’s name is a very subtle, yet powerful way to win people over. So the next time you meet someone and you want to quickly win their favor be sure to remember their name and use it often in conversation.


Look At People’s Feet

Former FBI agent Joe Navarro says that out of all our body parts, our feet are the most honest parts of our body. So the next time you’re standing and talking with someone, look at where their feet are pointing. You’ll discover some of the most revealing nonverbal information from that person just by looking at their feet.


Mise En Place

In the culinary arts, professional chefs have a term they use called “mise en place,” which is French for “put in place.” Like professional chefs, Wood recommends trying to reduce the friction needed to do your desired habit.

For instance:

  • If you want to eat better, then prepare healthy breakfast, lunch, and dinner meals in advance.
  • If you want to exercise in the morning, then lay out your workout clothes the night before.
  • If you want to read more, then put a book on your bed.

If you can reduce the friction for the positive habits that you want to build, then it won’t be as hard for you to build life-changing habits into your life.


Don’t Be A Donkey

“A donkey can’t think of the future. If he did, he’d realize he could clearly go first to drink the water, then go eat the hay. So my advice to my 30-year-old self is, don’t be a donkey. You can do everything you want to do. You just need foresight and patience.”


Therefore, if you have 10 things you want to accomplish over the next 10 years, just know that you can definitely achieve those 10 things. But all you have to do is simply dedicate yourself to one thing for a year. And then dedicate yourself to the next thing for another year. And so on. However, if you try to do all 10 things at once, then you’re going to end up like a donkey and not achieve anything. Don’t be a donkey.


Stop Using The Number 7

Why does Tim Ferriss say you’re not allowed to use 7? Because 7 is too safe of a number. 7 doesn’t commit to anything. If you rate something a 7, there’s a good chance you’ll feel obligated to say yes to it when you shouldn’t. Whereas, if you rate something a 6 (terrible) or an 8 (exciting), it’s a lot easier to quickly decide whether or not you should even consider it. The benefit of making decisions this way is that it forces you to make a decision. This is a method you can use for anything, whether it’s deciding if you should buy a specific book, go to a conference, or have a coffee chat with someone. Don’t be scared to have an opinion. Stop playing it safe. Make a decision.


Be A Whiner

“I’m sure there have been many other things I have whined about in the past, and many more that I will whine about in the future. What I don’t understand is why so many people think whining has a negative connotation. I don’t. Whining is the first step toward change. It’s the moment when you realize something is very wrong and that you have to take the initiative to do something about it… People who don’t whine are punching bags. They just go about their days, their jobs, their lives, knowing there is nothing they can do to change a darn thing, so why say a word? They see no reason to whine because they know they are incapable of effecting change. Call me a whiner any day.”


Take Sabbaticals From Your Work

If you ever feel like you’re experiencing creative roadblocks in your work or that you’re feeling burnt out, it’s probably time to take a sabbatical.

What’s a sabbatical? Sabbaticals are mini-vacations from your work, which are meant to act as a detox from your daily routine so that you can recharge and get back to work better than before.

Taking a sabbatical, whether it’s for a week, a day, or even just a few hours, is a great way to cultivate new ideas, to experience fewer creative blocks, and to avoid burnout in your work.


Never Ask For Someone’s ‘Opinion’

If you ever want to ask someone for input about an idea you have, then never ask for their “opinion.” Instead, always ask for their “advice.”

The differential phrasing might seem minor, but in the book “Pre-Suasion” psychology and marketing professor Robert Cialdini says that asking for ‘advice’ can have a significant positive impact in getting other people to provide you feedback as well as getting other people to want to work with you.


Practice What’s It’s Like To Be Poor

For many of us, we constantly worry about not having enough money. We fear what life will look like if we can’t afford the things we think we want and are forced to live on just the bare necessities.

But oftentimes this fear paralyzes us and keeps us from being as happy and successful as we could be.

But instead of constantly worrying about what might go wrong if you were to get fired from your job or your business was to fail, why not rehearse what each potential fear-inducing moment would be like before it ever happens?

This is a psychological technique known as “fear rehearsing,” which is where you regularly microdose yourself with the worst case scenario as a way to desensitize yourself to your fears.













Creating habit

Troubleshooter

  1. Are you forgetting to do your habits?
  2. Can't motive yourself to start? (temptention bundle - mix habits you like and you dislike)
  3. Too difficult?
  4. Is your habit getting easier to stick to over time?
  5. Designing your environment for success
  6. The 2 minute rule for the start of habits
  7. Master the entry points/ first step for habits.
  8. Join a community Whos normal habit is your desired habit
  9. Use variable rewards- most bad habits have immediate rewards and long term consequences. Most good habits are the exact opposite- reward system example: jar of marbles 90 red & 10 blue, after every good habit practice pull out a marble, if red then nothing, if blue then reward thyself.


Studies

Make intentions and plan

Research has shown that you are 2x to 3x more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan for when, where, and how you will perform the behavior. For example, in one study scientists asked people to fill out this sentence: “During the next week, I will partake in at least 20 minutes of vigorous exercise on [DAY] at [TIME OF DAY] at/in [PLACE].”


Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were 2x to 3x more likely to actually exercise compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior. Psychologists call these specific plans “implementation intentions” because they state when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior.


This finding is well proven and has been repeated in hundreds studies across a broad range of areas. For example, implementation intentions have been found to increase the odds that people will start exercising, begin recycling, stick with studying, and even stop smoking.


However (and this is crucial to understand) follow-up research has discovered implementation intentions only work when you focus on one thing at a time. In fact, researchers found that people who tried to accomplish multiple goals were less committed and less likely to succeed than those who focused on a single goal.


This is important, so let me repeat: developing a specific plan for when, where, and how you will stick to a new habit will dramatically increase the odds that you will actually follow through, but only if you focus on one thing.


Mental habits

Destroy your limiting beliefs - be open-minded

We all have limiting beliefs, often pplaced deep in our brains from childhood. These limiting beliefs will hold you back even when you don't know they exist. They're the exact reason you self sabotage.

Limit comparison

There's nothing wrong with comparison to your competition. So long as you realise that the relative positioning to your competition does not dictate your self worth.

Correct yourslef - positive talk

You will oftne catch yourself saying something like "I'm not good at that" or "I'm not disciplined". Stop it. Correct yourself as soon as you catch yourself. You are programming yourself and sabotage to be better.

Remove toxicity

Tis goes for both online and in person. You will be undoubtedtly have toxic people in your life whether they gaslight you or just straight up put you down.

Be conscious of you body

Stand up straight, shoulders back, head high. A confident person does not walk with their head down back slumped.

Harden your body

If you harden your body, your mind will be hardened too. You will gain confidence from knowing that you are strong and capable of things that not many people is.

Build momentum

If you create momentum you have power to go throught all day and make things done. You should start with small things.

Control your ego

Realise that people will have opposing opinions. That's okay, that's good. Without opposing opinions life would be boring and nothing new would be discovered. You should tolerate their opinions and acknowledge that no everyone will understand you.

Delay gratification

The ability to delay gratification can be a big predictor of success. Mentally strong people have the ability to prioritize the long-term over short-term pleasures.

Show up on the toughest days

Often it's the days when we don't feel like showing up that end up being the most important ones. Proving to yourself that you can show up on tough days build your resilience and mental strength.

Don't dwell on things

Allowing a problem or situation to dominate your mind, is another quick way to lose resilience. Mentally strong people focus on what is within their control, and take action on it as soon as possible.



Philosophy


Essentialism

What it is?

Essentialism is a philosophy of life focused on doing less but better. It encourages individuals to prioritize what truly matters, eliminate non-essential distractions, and commit only to the activities and responsibilities that align with their core values and goals. It is not about getting more things done, but getting the right things done.

“Essentialism is not about how to get more things done; it’s about how to get the right things done.”
— Greg McKeown, author of Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less


„Jeśli nie można zdecydowanie powiedzieć 'tak’, należy zdecydowanie powiedzieć 'nie'” 


Historical background

While the modern popularization of Essentialism is largely credited to Greg McKeown's book (2014), the roots of Essentialist thinking can be traced back to ancient Stoicism, Buddhism, and minimalist traditions:

  • Stoics like Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius emphasized clarity of purpose and virtue over material distraction.
  • Buddhism promotes detachment from desires and focusing on what truly matters (spiritual growth).
  • Thoreau’s Walden (1854) reflected essentialist ideals: "Simplify, simplify."

Characteristics

  • Prioritization: Focus on a small number of truly important things.
  • Saying No: A disciplined rejection of anything non-essential.
  • Clarity: A clear understanding of what is important and aligned with your purpose.
  • Deliberate Action: Doing fewer things but with greater intent and excellence.
  • Boundaries: Protecting time and energy from constant demands.

Core values

Value

Description

Simplicity

Removing clutter—mental, emotional, physical.

Intentionality

Acting purposefully instead of reacting to everything.

Clarity

Knowing one’s values, goals, and mission.

Focus

Concentrating on the vital few instead of the trivial many.

Freedom

Choosing what to give attention to and saying “no” to the rest.

Key principles

  1. Explore and Evaluate: What is truly essential?
  2. Eliminate: Cut out the non-essentials.
  3. Execute: Build a system for effortless productivity on what matters.

Benefits

  • Reduced stress and overwhelm.
  • Higher productivity with meaningful outcomes.
  • Improved decision-making and clarity.
  • More time for rest, creativity, and personal growth.
  • Stronger sense of purpose and fulfillment.

Drawbacks or challenges

  • May be seen as selfish or rigid when saying "no" to others.
  • Requires discipline and uncomfortable trade-offs.
  • Not always feasible in chaotic or dependent environments (e.g., parenting, caregiving).
  • Misapplication may lead to undercommitment or excessive minimalism.

For who

Essentialism benefits:

  • Overwhelmed professionals juggling too many tasks.
  • Entrepreneurs seeking clarity and impact.
  • Knowledge workers looking to avoid burnout.
  • Minimalists or those pursuing intentional living.
  • Leaders who want to drive high-impact change with limited resources.

Practical applications

  • Declutter your calendar by removing unimportant meetings.
  • Use the “Hell Yes or No” rule: If it’s not a definite YES, it’s a NO.
  • Conduct weekly or monthly Essential Reviews—what’s aligned and what needs elimination?
  • Set non-negotiable time blocks for what matters most.
  • Regularly ask: Is this the most valuable use of my time and energy?


Stoicism

What it is?

“Of all people only those are at leisure who make time for philosophy, only they truly live. Not satisfied to merely keep good watch over their own days, they annex every age to their own. All the harvest of the past is added to their store. ” — Seneca


Stoicism is an ancient Greco-Roman philosophy of life that teaches individuals to achieve inner peace and resilience by focusing on what they can control and accepting what they cannot. It emphasizes virtue, rationality, self-discipline, and emotional clarity.


“We suffer more in imagination than in reality.”
— Seneca


“You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.”
— Marcus Aurelius

Historical background

  • Origin: Founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium.
  • Flourished in Hellenistic Greece and later in Rome.

  • Key Roman Stoics include:

    • Seneca (advisor to Nero, writer on ethics),
    • Epictetus (a former slave, teacher of Stoic thought),
    • Marcus Aurelius (Roman Emperor, author of Meditations).

The name "Stoicism" comes from the Stoa Poikile (Painted Porch) in Athens where Zeno taught.

Characteristics

  • Dichotomy of Control: Distinguishing between what we can and cannot control.
  • Virtue is the highest good: Living with wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance.
  • Emotional resilience: Managing emotions through rational thought.
  • Focus on present: Practicing mindfulness and accepting the moment.
  • Amor Fati: Loving one’s fate — embracing life as it is.

Core values

Value

Description

Wisdom

Understanding the world and acting accordingly.

Courage

Facing adversity and discomfort with strength.

Justice

Acting fairly and treating others with respect.

Temperance

Exercising self-control and moderation.

Acceptance

Embracing things outside of your control.

Resilience

Enduring hardship without complaint.

Key practices

  1. Negative visualization (premeditatio malorum): Imagining worst-case scenarios to prepare emotionally.
  2. Daily journaling: Reflection and self-examination (e.g., Meditations).
  3. Voluntary discomfort: Practicing hardship to build discipline.
  4. Memento Mori: Remembering mortality to value time and life.
  5. View from above: Taking a broader perspective to reduce ego and emotional turmoil.

Benefits

  • Improved emotional control and mental clarity.
  • Resilience in the face of adversity.
  • Strong moral compass and personal ethics.
  • Detachment from external validation and outcomes.
  • Greater inner peace and life satisfaction.

Drawbacks or challenges

  • May appear emotionally detached or cold to others.
  • Risk of overemphasizing control and underappreciating emotion.
  • Can be misinterpreted as passive acceptance of injustice.
  • Some concepts may feel rigid or too austere in modern life.

For who

Stoicism benefits:

  • Leaders, entrepreneurs, and professionals facing pressure and responsibility.
  • Individuals going through hardship or personal crises.
  • People seeking emotional strength and mental toughness.
  • Those interested in self-discipline, ethical living, or philosophy-based self-improvement.

Practical applications

  • Reframe setbacks as training for virtue.
  • Start a Stoic journal — reflect on your responses to events each day.
  • Use the “Is this in my control?” test when reacting to situations.
  • Read Meditations (Marcus Aurelius), Letters from a Stoic (Seneca), or Discourses (Epictetus).
  • Practice silence, reflection, and measured responses in difficult conversations.

Principles

The Stoic philosophy changed over time, shifting focus from logic and physics - to more psychological concerns like tranquility and well-being. Also, the Stoics could never convene to affirm all of their tenants precisely, but there are certain principles at the core of the Stoic operating system. Here are some of the most important beliefs and strategies that the Stoics recommend to live a better life.


“Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be One.”
– Marcus Aurelius


As the philosophy developed, the Stoics came to have very little patience for purely theoretical contemplation. They focused less on pondering for the sake of it and more on real-world pragmatism.


In the real world, you need to arrive at an answer and take action. A true Stoic is not an “armchair philosopher,” but someone who gets out and lives by their theory.


Also in this quote, one can immediately see the Stoic concern for a righteous life. Stoics think that a good life is one of moral action. If you want to live well, you have got to be a morally just person.



“The chief task in life is simply this: to identify and separate matters so that I can say clearly to myself which are externals not under my control, and which have to do with the choices I actually control. Where then do I look for good and evil? Not to uncontrollable externals, but within myself to the choices that are my own…”
– Epictetus


Stoics acknowledge that people don’t have control over all, or even much, of what happens in life. And they emphasize that worrying about things outside of their control is unproductive, or even irrational to a person who wants to attain tranquility.


The Stoics would have us remind ourselves daily - to actively differentiate between what is and is not under control - to not waste energy over uncontrollable adverse events.


Where many people worry endlessly about things out of their control, the Stoics think their energy is better spent thinking of creative solutions to problems, rather than the issues themselves.


“No person has the power to have everything they want, but it is in their power not to want what they don’t have, and to cheerfully put to good use what they do have.”
– Seneca


Living as a Stoic does not mean you must live without material goods. In fact, the Stoics think that material goods are just - to the extent that they serve your happiness and ability to live virtuously.


However, Stoics are hyper-aware of the power of consumerism over their tranquility and decision-making. Many individuals spend a significant portion of their days upset about not having a more beautiful car or a bigger home, even though they have excellent health and more possessions than most.


Seneca was known to practice days of poverty, where he would fast and wear unfashionable clothing, to remind himself that people do not require luxuries to live a good life. All in all, individuals have enough to get by and be happy, yet they are upset about their lives because they maintain an insatiable desire for more.


Stoics consciously try not to suffer over what they lack. Instead, they guide their awareness towards gratitude for what they have.


“I judge you unfortunate because you have never lived through misfortune. You have passed through life without an opponent—no one can ever know what you are capable of, not even you.”
– Seneca


The Stoics take a very different view of misfortune than most people. They expect mishaps and use them as opportunities to hone their virtues. That is not to say that they are glad when troubles beset them, but they try not to lament them needlessly, and they actively seek benefit wherever possible.


Imagine breaking a leg and needing to sit in bed for four months while it heals. A Stoic would attempt to guide their thoughts away from useless “woe is me” rumination and focus instead on how they might do something productive while bedridden (e.g., write their first book). They would try to reframe the event as a way to cultivate their patience and become more creative.


 Where there is an adverse event, Stoics try not to let it ruin their tranquility, and instead, they try to derive character-building benefits wherever possible.


“External things are not the problem. It’s your assessment of them. Which you can erase right now.”
– Marcus Aurelius


The Stoic way of life has made its way into modern Psychology. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, or CBT, is based on the idea that how we think (cognition), how we feel (emotion) and how we act (behavior) all interact together. Specifically, our thoughts determine our feelings and our behavior. So Stoicism is an ancient thought that has been proven by modern psychological science!


 In many ways, one’s thoughts determine their experience of reality. For two people who undergo the same hardship, their differing assessment of that same misfortune can result in entirely different emotions and behaviors. Where one may feel utter despair at the loss of a job, another may feel liberated and hopeful about the opportunity.


Monitoring one’s inner critic towards greater optimism can be a  boon to psychological well-being. Remember, it is not the event itself that makes one upset, but one’s thoughts about it.


“Let us prepare our minds as if we’d come to the very end of life. Let us postpone nothing. Let us balance life’s books each day. … The one who puts the finishing touches on their life each day is never short of time.”
- Seneca


“Keep death and exile before your eyes each day, along with everything that seems terrible— by doing so, you’ll never have a base thought nor will you have excessive desire.”
- Epictetus


“Memento Mori” has been an important concept in many philosophies, from the Stoics to the Existentialists. It means “remember that you will die.” While this may seem morbid, Stoics like Epictetus & Seneca believed that contemplating one’s mortality can lead to more gratitude and virtuous action.


Instead of always wanting more, this exercise reminds the Stoic to appreciate what they have, while they have it. Or in other words, Stoic philosophy can help you appreciate good like health and well-being while they have them.


When one remembers that their lives are not infinite, it tends to clarify what is really important. This idea is often summed up as advice given in the form of “You could get hit but a bus tomorrow.” Again it seems morbid, but the point is to get out and live today. Don’t stress so much about the little things, and ensure that you carpe that diem, as you won’t always have another chance.


“The good or ill of a man lies within his own will.”
- Epictetus


It ought to be said at least once more - that virtue is the primary concern of the practicing Stoic. More important than wealth or even health, excellence of character is the highest good.


A Stoic thinks that as long as they think and behave virtuously (things which are always under their control), that they need not concern themselves with the impact of external events that lay outside of their control.


Whether or not people are rude or one experiences an unending streak of bad luck is irrelevant, as long as the Stoic responds in virtuous ways - he/she can rest easy in knowing that they’re living a good life.








Amor fati

What it is?

Amor fati is a Latin phrase that may be translated as "love of fate" or "love of one's fate". It is used to describe an attitude in which one sees everything that happens in one's life, including suffering and loss, as good or, at the very least, necessary.


Filozofia Nietzschego

Głównym popularyzatorem koncepcji amor fati jest Fryderyk Nietzsche. Stwierdza on, że człowiek niejako ma obowiązek umiłowania losu, który jest nierozerwalnie związany z jego egzystencją. W formule amor fati niemiecki filozof stawia przed człowiekiem nie lada wyzwanie. Los, który mamy umiłować, obfituje zarówno w chwile największej radości, jak również w momenty najczarniejszej rozpaczy.


Koncepcja umiłowania losu zmienia ludzkie ujęcie rzeczywistości: z absurdalnej przypadkowości na złudne poczucie konieczności wszystkiego, co się wydarza. Amor fati może być impulsem do zmiany nastawienia do życia i świata, lecz jej trwałe obowiązywanie uzależnione jest jedynie od wiary człowieka w tę ideę.


Ja sam nie cierpiałem nigdy z powodu tego wszystkiego; co konieczne, nie dotyka mnie; amor fati jest moją najwewnętrzniejszą naturą – pisał Nietzsche.


Premeditatio malorum

What it is?

“What is quite unlooked for is more crushing in its effect, and unexpectedness adds to the weight of a disaster. This is a reason for ensuring that nothing ever takes us by surprise. We should project our thoughts ahead of us at every turn and have in mind every possible eventuality instead of only the usual course of events…

Rehearse them in your mind: exile, torture, war, shipwreck. All the terms of our human lot should be before our eyes.”

— Seneca

Premeditatio malorum (“the pre-meditation of evils”) is a Stoic exercise of imagining things that could go wrong or be taken away from us. It helps us prepare for life’s inevitable setbacks and develop resilience in the face of uncertainty. We don’t always get what is rightfully ours, even if we’ve earned it. Not everything is as clean and straightforward as we think they may be. Psychologically, we must prepare ourselves for this to happen.

Practice

  1. Identify Potential Challenges:

    • Reflect on various aspects of your life (work, relationships, health, etc.).
    • Think about what could go wrong in each area. These could range from minor inconveniences to significant setbacks.

  2. Visualize the Scenarios:

    • Close your eyes and vividly imagine these negative events happening.
    • Try to feel the emotions associated with these events, such as fear, sadness, or frustration.

  3. Consider Your Responses:

    • Think about how you would react to each scenario.
    • Plan your responses and strategies for dealing with these challenges effectively.

  4. Reframe Your Perspective:

    • Remind yourself that these events, while unpleasant, are not insurmountable.
    • Focus on what you can control and how you can grow from these experiences.

  5. Regular Practice:

    • Make Premeditatio Malorum a regular part of your routine, such as during daily meditation or journaling.

Examples

  1. Career:

    • Scenario: You lose your job unexpectedly.
    • Visualization: Imagine receiving the news and the immediate feelings of shock and worry.
    • Response: Consider the steps you would take next, such as updating your resume, reaching out to your network, and applying for new jobs. Think about how you would manage your finances in the interim.

  2. Health:

    • Scenario: You or a loved one faces a serious illness.
    • Visualization: Picture the diagnosis and the impact on daily life.
    • Response: Plan how you would seek medical advice, adjust your lifestyle, and offer support to your loved one. Reflect on maintaining a positive outlook and finding strength in difficult times.

  3. Relationships:

    • Scenario: A close relationship ends.
    • Visualization: Envision the conversation and the emotional aftermath.
    • Response: Think about how you would cope with the loss, such as seeking support from friends and family, focusing on self-care, and gradually moving forward.

  4. Financial:

    • Scenario: You encounter a major financial setback, like an unexpected expense or a market crash.
    • Visualization: Imagine the stress and the impact on your budget.
    • Response: Consider how you would adjust your spending, find additional income sources, and rebuild your savings.
