Ichigo ichie

Co to?

Ichigo ichie, czyli japońska sztuka przeżywania niesamowitych chwil, to filozofia mająca być odpowiedzią na współczesne, coraz szybsze tempo życia. Każdego dnia dociera do nas większa ilość bodźców.


Oczekiwania społeczeństwa, własne ambicje, a także rosnący konsumpcjonizm sprawiają, że coraz trudniej jest nam cieszyć się małymi momentami, przez co w efekcie nie przeżywamy „tu i teraz”, żyjąc w zawieszeniu pomiędzy wspomnieniami z przeszłości a planami na swoją przyszłość.

Główne zasady

Japońska sztuka jest zatem przede wszystkim prostą nauką świadomego doświadczania momentu, w którym aktualnie się znajdujemy, celebrowania go i wyciągania z niego esencji. Poznajcie 10 głównych zasad ichigo ichie:

Nie odkładaj specjalnych momentów na potem 

Innymi słowy jest to życie zgodnie z filozofią „teraz albo nigdy”. Życie niejednokrotnie podsuwa nam bowiem wyjątkowe okazje, a rzeczywistość weryfikuje nakreślone wcześniej plany. Japończycy wierzą, że powinniśmy korzystać z tych małych przypadków, czerpiąc z nich tyle, ile się da, akceptując to, co staje nam na drodze i próbując świadomie z tego korzystać.

Celebruj małe momenty tak, jakby już nigdy miały się nie wydarzyć

Każdy moment jest unikalny i tak naprawdę przydarza się tylko raz. Jeżeli pozwolimy mu ulecieć, nie poświęcając na to swojej uwagi, nie będzie już do tego powrotu. Każde spotkanie z drugim człowiekiem, każde nowo poznane miejsce wedle filozofii Japończyków powinniśmy zatem traktować tak, jakby było ono tym jedynym, które już nigdy się nie powtórzy, próbując wyciągnąć z niego to, co najcenniejsze.

Rób rzeczy, których nigdy wcześniej nie robiłeś

Jest to związane z doświadczaniem i przeżywaniem życia, odkrywaniem różnych jego aspektów. Powtarzając każdorazowo te same czynności nie jesteśmy bowiem w stanie uzyskać innych niż poprzednio rezultatów. Ichigo ichie skłania nas do poszukiwania i odkrywania tego, co nieznane, a następnie świadomego doświadczania nowych rzeczy.

Zatop się w teraźniejszości

Przeszłości nie jesteśmy w stanie zmienić, więc pozostaje nam ją zaakceptować. Przyszłość jest jedną wielką niewiadomą, a drobny przypadek sprawić może, że nasze mnogie plany nigdy nie zostaną zrealizowane, a to, o co najbardziej się martwimy, być może nigdy się nie wydarzy. Jedynym, na co mamy faktyczny, bezpośredni wpływ, jest teraźniejszość. Warto ją zatem docenić, zaakceptować i spróbować wykorzystać jak najlepiej.

Medytuj 

Esencją medytacji jest bowiem zatopienie się w teraźniejszości, odsunięcie od siebie zbędnych myśli na temat tego co było lub będzie, zrobienie kroku wstecz, aby z dystansem i bez zbędnego oceniania obserwować i poczuć otaczające nas „tu i teraz”. Medytacja naturalnie wpisuje się zatem w filozofię ichigo ichie, a dodatkowo ma niezwykle korzystny wpływ zarówno na zdrowie psychiczne, jak i fizyczne, co potwierdzają liczne badania.

Świadomie korzystaj ze swoich zmysłów 

Dotyk, wzrok, węch, smak, umiejętność słuchania. Uważność na docierające do nas bodźce, ich świadome filtrowanie i doświadczanie może okazać się niezwykle cenną umiejętnością, która sprawi, że dostrzeżemy w życiu rzeczy, które w natłoku spraw umykały wcześniej naszej świadomości.

Dostrzeż przypadek

Życie to suma wydarzających się przypadków, o czym pewnie niejednokrotnie przekonał się każdy z nas. Nawet najlepiej dopracowany plan może szybko zostać zweryfikowany przez rzeczywistość. Japończycy wierzą, że każdy przypadek ma swoje znaczenie i tak naprawdę nic nie dzieje się przypadkowo, a naszym zadaniem jest nauczyć się odczytywać sygnały wysyłane nam przez wszechświat.

Nie wyczekuj w życiu specjalnych momentów

Specjalnym momentem jest „tu i teraz”. Permanentne oczekiwanie weekendu, wakacji, konkretnego wydarzenia sprawiają tylko, że nie jesteśmy w stanie skupić się na teraźniejszości i świadomie jej przeżywać. Według ichigo ichie powinniśmy raczej spróbować uczynić każdy mały moment wielkim i wartym wyjątkowego celebrowania.

Jeżeli nie podoba Ci się rzeczywistość, w której żyjesz, zmień ją 

Każdy z nas ma nieograniczoną możliwość kreowania własnej rzeczywistości, świadomego otaczania się ludźmi i dobierania swoich myśli. Japońska filozofia mówi także o tym, że świadomość i akceptacja jest pierwszym krokiem do ewentualnej zmiany, a być może ta okaże się niezbędna. Siła człowieka i jego wpływu na rzeczywistość są z kolei niezmierzone.

Praktyka czyni mistrza 

Każdego dnia próbuj chwytać szczególne momenty. Poszukaj ich pijąc poranną kawę, stojąc w korku, rozmawiając z kolegą z pracy czy wyglądając przez okno. Spróbuj nadać tym małym rzeczom szczególne znaczenie i traktuj je tak, jakby były one wszystkim, co teraz masz. Celebruj codzienność, nie wyczekując wielkich zdarzeń, a doceniając wartość tych małych.


Wabi-sabi

Co to?

Jeden z estetycznych zmysłów Japonii, sztuka odnajdywania piękna w niedoskonałości, w rzeczach prostych i skromnych, celebracja piękna normalności i autentyczności, mądrość naturalnej prostoty i wyzwolenie od uprzedzeń, surowy spokój, elegancka prostota.


Pierwotnie wabi i sabi miały różne znaczenia, ale obecnie zlały się w jedno, zapisywane wabi-sabi, oznaczające piękno odnajdywane w spokojnej prostocie i ascetycznym wyrafinowaniu. Mówi się, że jest to centralna ideologia kultury japońskiej.


WABI SABI ma jednak o wiele szerszy aspekt, niż tylko czysto-estetyczny.

Nieodwracalny upływ czasu i przemijanie zostają wreszcie odarte ze strachu i obdarzone spokojem i akceptacją.


Melancholijne piękno tkwiące w nietrwałości wszystkich rzeczy przestaje być wstydliwie skrywane.


Taken individually, wabi and sabi are two separate concepts:

  • Wabi is about recognizing beauty in humble simplicity. It invites us to open our heart and detach from the vanity of materialism so we can experience spiritual richness instead.
  • Sabi is concerned with the passage of time, the way all things grow, age, and decay, and how it manifests itself beautifully in objects. It suggests that beauty is hidden beneath the surface of what we actually see, even in what we initially perceive as broken.

Principles

According to Zen philosophy, wabi sabi rests on seven aesthetic principles:

  1. Kanso — simplicity
  2. Fukinsei — asymmetry or irregularity
  3. Shibumi — the beauty of the understated
  4. Shizen — naturalness without pretension
  5. Yugen — subtle grace
  6. Datsuzoku — freeness
  7. Seijaku — tranquility


Key to all seven of these aesthetic pillars is authenticity. Unadorned naturalness is prized for its integrity, free of synthetic artifice. Beauty is expressed through the open display of flaws rather than their eradication. Compassion for ourselves and others, and acceptance of our vulnerability are also elements of the wabi sabi mindset.

Teachings

Through acceptance, you find freedom; out of acceptance, you find growth

The core philosophy of their training can be summed in one word, Uketamo, which means "I humbly accept with an open heart."

Here’s how it works:

  • You’re about to lose your job? Uketamo.
  • The forecast suddenly changed to downpour rain and now you must cancel your outdoor event? Uketamo.
  • You had a very silly accident and now you’ve fractured your left leg and are due to be in a cast for the next month? Uketamo.

Uketamo means acceptance to the core. The Yamabushi understood that the sooner you can accept all the good and bad things life throws at you, the lighter you will feel. They fathomed that we find our freedom through acceptance, and out of acceptance, we find our path to growth.


The idea is quite simple: As you continue to resist, so will you continue to compound your suffering.

The first teaching of the wabi-sabi philosophy, then, is to practice gratitude and acceptance. It’s not about giving up. It’s about surrendering to the gravity of the situation at hand and then actively playing a role in deciding what happens next.


Uketamo reminds me of what the Stoics called Amor Fati, a love of fate. And Wabi-sabi preaches the same: You will find peace and freedom, and you will step onto the path of growth, once you begin yielding and surrendering to the imperfect flow of life.

All things in life, including you, are in an imperfect state of flux, so strive not for perfection, but for excellence instead

If everything in nature is always changing, then nothing can ever be absolutely complete. And since perfection is a state of completeness, then nothing can ever be perfect. Hence, the wabi-sabi philosophy teaches us that all things, including us and life itself, are impermanent, incomplete, and imperfect.


The problem, however, is that our flawed ways of thinking have now blurred our understanding of what perfection really is.


Open up a thesaurus and search for the antonyms for "perfect" and you’ll find the following words: Flawed, corrupt, inferior, poor, second-rate, inept, broken, wrong, bad… My goodness. All this negativity. No wonder we’ve become so obsessed with seeking perfection.


We sculpt the perfect body, based on what society deems it must look like to pass that test of perfection. We seek the perfect career path and the perfect partner based on someone else’s definition of that perfection. And as creators, we procrastinate until eternity before ever releasing that imperfect piece of art.


But here’s the reality check: Perfection does not exist because imperfection is the natural state of life—you are whole, the entirety of you, as you are.


In order to eliminate this negative stigma around imperfection, we first need to completely reject it as being “the opposite” of that fictional construct that is perfection. We need to write a new narrative that reads: Imperfection is not a compromise; imperfection is the only way because imperfection is the true nature of things.


The second teaching of the wabi-sabi philosophy is simple: Strive not for perfection, but for excellence instead.


In other words, simply do your best to be the best that you can be.

Appreciate the beauty of all things, especially the great beauty that hides beneath the surface of what seems to be broken

An ancient form of art stems from wabi-sabi, whereby you mend broken objects with gold fillings, giving them “golden scars.” It’s known as Kintsugi.


Think of a bowl or teapot that has been dropped onto the floor. What would you do with it? You’d most probably pick up the pieces and throw them away. But not with Kintsugi. Here, you bring the pieces of broken pottery back together and glue them with liquid gold. Wouldn’t that make them imperfect, permanently and inevitably flawed, but somehow, more beautiful?


Kintsugi reminds us that there is great beauty in broken things because scars tell a story. They demonstrate fortitude, wisdom, and resilience, earned through the passage of time. Why hide these imperfections or golden scars when we are meant to celebrate them?


The idea here is simple: There will be many times in your life when you will feel broken. There will be events that will leave you with emotional or physical scars. Do not hide in the shadow of your own sunshine. Do not dim your own light with the darkness of a cloud. Instead, let those scars be redrawn with gold.


Slow and simple, is the only way, to feel the joy of what it means to be alive

You might be wondering, but how can you see the beauty beneath the surface? How do you manage to find beauty in everyday life when everything seems so dark and grim?


The answer to those questions lies in the philosophy’s fourth teaching: Slow down and simplify your life. Otherwise, you’ll rush through it, arrive at the end and wonder, “what was the point?” This teaching is quite simple, but its immediate and long-term implications are profound.


Here’s why:

  1. Slowing down is the antidote to living in a rhythm of rush. Slowing down is what helps you become a more observant person. Which then helps you become more self-aware. Why? Because as soon as you slow down, you begin creating the space for you to pause and reflect, to wonder and ask questions. You naturally become more present. Why do you think most people hit rock bottom or total burnout before it finally dawns on them that their way of life is not sustainable? It’s because they were moving too fast and never slowed down to carve out the mental and emotional space for them to observe and analyze their self-sabotaging behaviour.
  2. Simplifying your life is the antidote to living a complex one. At any point in time, as soon as you seek to change something in your life, you will, time and again, realize that the first step is not to ask, “what do I need to add,” but “what do I need to remove?” When you’re about to move into a new home, you throw out some old stuff. When you’re budgeting, you stip away the needless expenses. When you’re entering a new relationship, you wonder, what are some habits that I need to let go, so that I can make way for this person into my life. Decluttering is an integral part of the journey to growth and change. Letting of what no longer serves you is how you allow room for what will.

Slow and simple is the only way to feel the joy of what it means to be alive. Why? Because only by doing so will you allow yourself to become more present and in tune with the world around you. Only by doing so will you immerse yourself into the fabric of this universe and appreciate it for what it is: The joy of watering your flowers in the morning, the joy of watching a sinking sun, the joy listening to soft rain, the joy baking of a cake or reading a book under the share of a tree.


Beauty is found in everything that is alive.


To be content exactly where you are with all that you already have, is to be happy

Modern-day society is obsessed with finding happiness. Honestly, I was a victim of this myself. I spent a significant portion of my young adult life pursuing the next big thing: The next big job, the next big startup, the next big move to a new country. And every time I overworked myself to arrive at where I thought I wanted to be, this wave of emptiness washed over me.


This wave of hopelessness is what Harvard positive psychology, Tal Ben-Shahar, coined as the arrival fallacy, “the illusion that once we make it, once we attain our goal or reach our destination, we will reach lasting happiness.” But of course, that’s not the case, because compulsive goal-setting does not lead to happiness, it leads to a mindless and stressful game of fetch.


The truth is, our obsession with seeking happiness has blinded us to what happiness actually is: An emotion.


It’s just another emotion.


We feel happy and unhappy just as how we feel angry, sad, scared, or excited. You can’t be happy all the time just as how you can’t be excited all the time.


So what’s the problem with chasing happiness? First, it will always evade you. And second, it’s virtually impossible to be happy all the time.


This is where the final wabi-sabi teaching comes in.


On a 17th-century tsukubai (water basin) stone at the Ryoanji Temple in Kyoto, there’s an ancient inscription where four Chinese characters are written on the stone. Read alone, these characters are of no significance. But when combined with the borders of the central square, they can be read as "ware tada taru wo shiru,” which means “I only know plenty,” or “I only know contentment.”

I only know contentment.


Isn’t that so powerful?


To be content with the emotion of anger just as how you are usually content with the emotion of excitement. To be content with the state of sadness just as how you are incredibly content with the state of happiness.


But how about a more poetic translation to that inscription?

How about, “rich is the person who is content with who he is or what he has.” Or, how about this: “What I have is all I need.”


You see, the root of all unhappiness is born from being discontent with where you are and what you have. It really is as simple as that.


The root of all unhappiness is born from spending all your waking hours casting your gaze out into the distant future and looking outside your life, instead of opening your eyes to the present and looking inside it.


To be content with what you have and where you are is to be grateful. To be content with what you have and where you are, while working toward what you want, and fully trusting that you can achieve it, is to be intentional. And through gratitude, intention, and action, you find happiness.


But the beauty of it all? It circles back to the first wabi-sabi teaching: Acceptance is contentment and contentment is acceptance.




Shikita ga nai

What it is?

The concept of "Shikata ga nai" embodies the Japanese cultural attitude of accepting situations that are beyond one's control or cannot be changed. It reflects a mindset of stoicism, resilience, and a pragmatic approach to life's challenges. The phrase suggests that, rather than dwelling on the impossibility of altering a particular outcome, it's more productive to acknowledge the situation, accept it, and find a way to move forward.


"Shikata ga nai" doesn't imply passivity or indifference; instead, it encourages individuals to focus on what they can control and take positive steps despite the adversity. It aligns with the Japanese value of endurance, emphasizing the importance of maintaining composure and adapting to circumstances.


This concept is deeply rooted in Japanese culture and history, particularly in the face of natural disasters, social challenges, or personal setbacks. It reflects a collective resilience and a belief in facing difficulties with grace and determination. While it can be seen as a cultural trait, individuals from various backgrounds may appreciate and apply the principle of "Shikata ga nai" as a way to navigate the inevitable uncertainties of life.



Gaman

What it is?

The concept of "gaman" (我慢) in Japanese culture refers to enduring or persevering with patience and dignity in the face of difficult or challenging situations. It involves the ability to tolerate and endure hardships without complaint, demonstrating self-control, resilience, and a sense of inner strength.


Key aspects of the "gaman" concept include:

  1. Endurance: "Gaman" emphasizes the strength to endure adversity without giving in to frustration or complaint. It involves maintaining composure in the face of difficulties.
  2. Patience: Patience is a central element of "gaman." It involves waiting for a positive outcome, understanding that change may take time, and avoiding impulsive reactions.
  3. Resilience: "Gaman" encourages resilience in the face of setbacks. It involves bouncing back from challenges, learning from experiences, and maintaining a positive outlook.
  4. Self-discipline: The concept involves self-discipline and self-control, recognizing that there are situations beyond one's control and choosing not to succumb to negative emotions.
  5. Dignity: "Gaman" is often associated with maintaining one's dignity and grace under pressure. It involves facing challenges with a sense of honor and integrity.
  6. Collectivism: In Japanese culture, "gaman" is also associated with a sense of collective endurance. People may endure challenges not just for personal reasons but also for the greater good of the community or family.


Examples of "gaman" in practice might include individuals enduring long work hours without complaining, students persevering through rigorous study schedules, or people coping with adversity after natural disasters without losing hope. The concept has historical roots in Japan and has been shaped by cultural, philosophical, and societal influences. "Gaman" reflects a cultural value that has been passed down through generations as a way of navigating life's difficulties with strength and resilience.



Shoshin

What it is?

Shoshin (Japanese: 初心) is a concept from Zen Buddhism meaning beginner's mind. It refers to having an attitude of openness, eagerness, and lack of preconceptions when studying, even at an advanced level, just as a beginner would. The term is especially used in the study of Zen Buddhism and Japanese martial arts, and was popularized outside of Japan by Shunryū Suzuki's 1970 book Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.


The Buddhist monk Shunryū Suzuki, who was the first to set up a monastery outside of Asia, summed up it in his book Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind:


"In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities… But in the expert's there are few".


Shoshin refers to adopting a mindset of humility and curiosity when approaching a subject — even if one is already at an advanced level. Some examples of Shoshin in action are:

  • Having a lack of preconceived notions when learning.
  • Actively seeking out opposing views.
  • An undying eagerness to learn.

I have taken the liberty to compile some tips that anyone can use to learn the Japanese concept of Shoshin. If applied, they will lead you to tremendous personal growth.


Beginner’s mind

The concept holds that those who approach life with few preconceptions will be open to new ideas and perspectives, while those who believe themselves experts will only see what affirms their own worldview – and may miss crucial learnings.


James Clear, New York Times bestselling author of Atomic Habits, explains: “Who is to say that the way you originally learned a skill is the best way? Most people think they are experts in a field, but they are really just experts in a particular style.


“In this way, we become a slave to our old beliefs without even realizing it. We adopt a philosophy or strategy based on what we have been exposed to without knowing if it's the optimal way to do things.

If rugby players took a formulaic approach to every game, expecting certain things to stay the same each time, based on their wealth of previous experience, they might miss the small windows of opportunity to score a try.



Oubaitori

What it is?

The ancient Japanese idiom, Oubaitori, comes from the kanji for the four trees that bloom in spring: cherry blossoms, plum, peach, and apricot. Each flower blooms in its own time, and the meaning behind the idiom is that we all grow and bloom at our own pace. It acts as a reminder that everyone has their own journey through life, and we should focus on our growth, and not compare ourselves so much to others, and to celebrate your individuality and your uniqueness.


Oubaitori emphasizes the beauty in uniqueness rather than comparison. Like the distinct flavors of peaches and plums, each life is unique with its own journey, values, choices, and experiences. Even genetically identical twins develop into different individuals, highlighting the futility of comparing ourselves to others.


Yet, we often compare our lives to the seemingly perfect ones portrayed on social media or successful young entrepreneurs, leading to feelings of inadequacy. We question why we face setbacks while others seem to prosper, forgetting that no two paths are alike and comparison only hinders our appreciation of our own unique journey.


Oubaitori is a refreshing change from the western craze of ‘’Keeping up with the Joneses”. The Oubaitori way is about enjoying a fulfilling life by doing what’s right for you, at the time and in the manner that is right for you.


Instead of moaning about what you lack, learn to capitalize on the strengths that you have been bestowed with. It’s for us to use the gifts we have, to maximize what we can do with our own life.


How to practise

  1. Be aware of your self-talk and be kind to yourself
  2. Stop talking negatively about yourself to others.
  3. Filter your social media
  4. Remind yourself you don’t have the full picture
  5. Establish a gratitude practice
  6. Use the success of others as motivation





Shuhari

What it is?

Shuhari (守破離) is a concept from Japanese martial arts encapsulating the journey towards mastery. It outlines the three stages of learning: Shu (守) emphasizes adhering to and preserving traditional wisdom; Ha (破) encourages deviation and innovation beyond traditions; and Ri (離) signifies transcending to a state where actions are fluid, intuitive, and unconstrained by formal structures.

While its origins are in aikido, the concept of shuhari has been popularized among agile software development circles by developers like Martin Fowler and Alistair Cockburn, and abstracted even more broadly to learning in general because it offers a framework for progressive learning and mastery.


Stages

  • Shu (守) "protect", "obey"-traditional wisdom: The beginning stage is focused solely on learning fundamentals through repetition. You repeat the basic forms until you form muscle memory. In the shu stage, you're not concerned with any underlying theory of the practice.
  • Ha (破) "detach", "digress"-breaking with tradition: Once you've mastered the basic forms and can begin to innovate. You might branch out and learn from other masters. Having an understanding of the underlying theory, you might incorporate methods and variations from outside sources into your own practice. 
  • Ri (離) "leave", "separate"-transcendence: In the final stage of mastery, you can depart from forms altogether and proceed however your mind desires. Your learning no longer comes from other people, but your own practice. When you've reached the ri stage, you are, in essence, expanding the discipline.


Applying Shuhari

This learning model can be applied across all sorts of disciplines and creative practices. Understanding where you land on the shuhari journey can make the process of learning both easier and less daunting.  

Most disciplines can be learned this way. In many cases, what we view as genius or talent are simply the result of a shuhari approach, especially in creative practices. Allowing yourself patience and tailoring your learning to the right stage will ultimately make the road to mastery much more enjoyable.




Isogaba maware


Kishi Kaisei

What it is?

"Kishi Kaisei" (起死回生) is a Japanese proverb that means "to revive from the brink of death" or "to come back to life after a close call." It's made up of two parts: "kishi" (起死), which means "waking from death," and "kaisei" (回生), which means "coming back to life." This phrase is often used to describe situations where there's a dramatic turnaround, like when someone recovers from a serious illness or when a team wins a game after being way behind. It's about making a comeback against the odds.

Applying

"Kishi Kaisei" is a Japanese phrase that means "wake from death and return to life." It's about making a comeback or recovering from a hopeless situation. Here are some examples of how it can be applied in life:


  1. School Comeback: Imagine you're getting really low grades in school. Instead of giving up, you work super hard, get help from teachers, and study more. By the end of the year, your grades have improved a lot. That's like a kishi kaisei!
  2. Sports Recovery: Let's say a soccer team is losing 3-0 at halftime. They could just quit, but instead, they pep-talk each other, change their strategy, and play their hearts out. They end up winning 4-3. That amazing turnaround is a perfect example of kishi kaisei.
  3. Health Turnaround: Someone might be very sick, maybe they haven't taken good care of their health. But then, they decide to eat better, exercise, and follow doctor's orders. Slowly, they get healthier and feel better. Their recovery is like a kishi kaisei moment.
  4. Business Revival: A small business might be close to failing because it's not making enough money. The owners could close shop, but instead, they try new ideas, advertise more, and improve their products. The business starts to do well again. That's kishi kaisei in action.
  5. Personal Growth: Maybe someone has a bad habit, like being super messy. One day, they decide to change. They start cleaning regularly and become more organized. Turning their habit around is kind of like kishi kaisei.


In all these cases, kishi kaisei is about not giving up, even when things look bad. It's about finding the strength to turn things around and make them better.

Mono no aware

What it is?

Mono no aware is a Japanese term that translates roughly to "the pathos of things." It describes the awareness of the impermanence of all things and the gentle sadness and wistfulness at their passing. The concept also encompasses a longer, deeper gentle sadness about this state being the reality of life. Mono no aware is a key part of Japanese culture and aesthetics, often linked to the beauty of cherry blossoms, which bloom brilliantly and then fade away quickly. It's an appreciation of the fleeting nature of beauty, encouraging people to cherish the transient moments in life.

How to practise?

Practicing "Mono no aware," a Japanese term that translates to "the pathos of things," involves developing an awareness of the impermanence of all things and a gentle sadness at their passing. Here are some steps to help you embrace this concept:

  1. Mindfulness

    • Take time each day to be present in the moment.
    • Notice the beauty in everyday objects and experiences.

  2. Appreciation of Nature

    • Spend time outdoors observing the changing seasons.
    • Reflect on the natural cycle of life and death.

  3. Art and Literature

    • Engage with art, poetry, and stories that capture fleeting beauty or poignant moments.
    • Create your own art expressing these themes.

  4. Reflection

    • Keep a journal to write down thoughts and feelings about experiences that move you.
    • Contemplate the transient nature of life and how it gives meaning to our experiences.

  5. Emotional Acceptance

    • Allow yourself to feel sadness for things that are lost or changing.
    • Recognize that this sadness is a part of appreciating the full range of human emotions.

  6. Letting Go

    • Practice letting go of attachments to physical objects, outcomes, or ideas.
    • Understand that change is inevitable and often beyond control.

  7. Cultural Exploration

    • Learn more about Japanese culture and how "Mono no aware" is expressed in traditions and festivals.
    • Participate in activities such as Hanami (cherry blossom viewing) which celebrate transient beauty.


By incorporating these practices into your daily life, you can begin to embody the spirit of "Mono no aware" and find a deeper connection to the world around you.

Nana koro bi ya oki

What it is?

The concept of "Nana korobi ya oki" (七転び八起き) is a Japanese proverb that translates to "Fall seven times, stand up eight." It means that no matter how many times you face setbacks or failures, you should always get back up and keep trying. The essence of this saying is resilience and perseverance, encouraging people to not give up despite difficulties or challenges.


Shogonai

What it is?

Shoganai, sometimes spelled "shou ga nai" or "shikata ga nai," is a Japanese phrase that translates to "it can't be helped" or "nothing can be done about it." It reflects a common attitude in Japanese culture towards situations that are beyond one's control. The concept encourages acceptance and resilience, suggesting that when faced with the unchangeable, it's better to adapt and move forward rather than resist or complain. This mindset is deeply rooted in the pragmatism and stoicism that are valued in Japanese society.


Ganbaru

What it is?

Ganbaru is a Japanese term that doesn't have a direct translation in English, but it roughly means to persevere or to stay committed to a task even when it's difficult. It's about putting in your best effort and showing determination and endurance. In Japanese culture, ganbaru is highly valued as it reflects a person's character and commitment to meeting their goals or responsibilities, no matter how challenging they may be.


Mushin

What it is?

Mushin is a Japanese concept often described as a state of "no-mindness." It's about reaching a mental state where the mind is free from thoughts, emotions, and judgments. This allows for a person to react to things without hesitation or disturbance from inner thoughts, often resulting in a state of mental clarity and fluid action. In martial arts, mushin is the ability to act naturally and effortlessly, without overthinking or emotional interference. It's closely related to the idea of being fully present in the moment and can be applied to various aspects of life, not just martial arts.


Shin-Gi-Tai

Introduction

The concept of Shin-Gi-Tai (心技体) is a traditional Japanese philosophical triad originally rooted in martial arts (Budo), but it has since evolved into a universal framework for peak performance, personal development, and mastery.

It suggests that true excellence is only achieved when Mind, Technique, and Body are in perfect equilibrium. If one is missing, the structure collapses.

心 (Shin) – Mind, Spirit, and Intent

The "Shin" is the engine of the triad. It represents your internal world—your psychological resilience, ethics, and emotional regulation.

  • The Psychology: This aligns with the concept of "Grit" (perseverance) and "Emotional Intelligence". It is the ability to stay calm under pressure (Fudoshin - the immovable mind).

  • Key Components:

    • Focus: The ability to direct your energy toward a single goal without distraction.
    • Determination: The "Will" to continue when the Body (Tai) is exhausted.
    • Ethical Compass: The "Spirit" aspect—ensuring your skills are used with integrity and purpose.
  • In Practice: Meditation, visualization, and stress-management techniques. It’s the "Why" behind your actions.

技 (Gi) – Technique, Skill, and Knowledge

"Gi" is the expression of your effort. It represents the hours of "Deep Practice" required to master a craft, whether it’s martial arts, business, or art.

  • The Psychology: This relates to "Procedural Memory" and the "Flow State". When your technique is so refined that it becomes instinctive, you no longer have to "think" about what to do.

  • Key Components:

    • Mastery: Understanding the fine details and mechanics of your craft.
    • Adaptability: The ability to apply your skills in different or unpredictable situations.
    • Continuous Learning: The "Shoshin" (Beginner’s Mind) approach—never assuming you know everything.
  • In Practice: Deliberate practice, studying theory, and constant refinement through feedback. It’s the "How" of your performance.

体 (Tai) – Body, Health, and Physicality

"Tai" is the vessel. Without a strong, healthy physical foundation, the Mind (Shin) loses its focus and the Technique (Gi) cannot be executed effectively.

  • The Psychology: Physical health directly impacts cognitive function. The "Biopsychosocial Model" shows that things like sleep, nutrition, and physical strength are the fuel for mental performance.

  • Key Components:

    • Conditioning: Strength, flexibility, and cardiovascular endurance.
    • Restoration: Proper sleep and recovery to prevent burnout.
    • Body Awareness: Understanding your physical limits and maintaining "Proprioception" (knowing where your body is in space).
  • In Practice: Nutrition, consistent exercise, and tactical recovery. It’s the "Hardware" that runs the software.

The Integration: Why Balance Matters

The magic of Shin-Gi-Tai happens at the intersection. Most people fail because they over-index on one at the expense of others:

  • Tai + Gi (No Shin): You are a powerful, skilled "machine," but you crumble under pressure or lack the moral direction to use your skills wisely.
  • Shin + Tai (No Gi): You have a strong spirit and a fit body, but you are "clumsy." You have the will to win, but not the tools to execute.
  • Shin + Gi (No Tai): You are brilliant and highly skilled, but you lack the "stamina" to finish the race. You burn out quickly or fall ill when the stakes are highest.

Nintai

Introduction

Nintai is a cornerstone of Japanese philosophy, representing the profound virtue of patience, perseverance, and fortitude. While often translated simply as "patience," the term encompasses a much deeper psychological and spiritual state: the ability to remain steadfast and composed in the face of suffering, provocation, or long-term hardship.

Etymology: The Blade over the Heart

The true essence of Nintai is found in the anatomy of its first Kanji character, Nin (忍).

  • The Upper Part (刃): Represents a "blade" or "sword."
  • The Lower Part (心): Represents the "heart" or "spirit."

The visual representation suggests a blade pressed against the heart. To practice Nintai is to maintain a "still heart" even when under extreme pressure or pain. It is the refusal to break, panic, or act impulsively when the situation is at its most critical. The second character, Tai (耐), adds the dimension of "resisting" or "bearing," reinforcing the idea of physical and mental stamina over time.

Psychology of Nintai: Emotional Regulation

In modern psychology, Nintai aligns closely with Delayed Gratification and Impulse Control.

  • The Gap Between Stimulus and Response: Nintai is the expansion of that gap. When someone insults you or a task becomes frustrating, Nintai allows you to observe the emotion without being swept away by it.
  • The "Slow Burn" of Mastery: Most people quit when the "honeymoon phase" of a new skill (the Gi) ends. Nintai is the psychological grit that allows you to push through the "plateau of latent potential"—that long period where you are working hard but seeing no results.

Three Dimensions of Nintai

I. Physical Endurance (Stamina)

This is the ability of the body to withstand external stressors—cold, heat, exhaustion, or physical discomfort—without the mind's resolve wavering. In many Japanese traditions, physical hardship is sought out specifically to "polish" the spirit.

II. Mental Fortitude (Persistence)

This refers to the "long-game" mindset. It is the capacity to work toward a goal for years without seeing immediate results. It is the antidote to the human tendency toward instant gratification. Nintai allows an individual to push through the "boring" or "plateau" phases of any pursuit.

III. Emotional Regulation (Composure)

Nintai is the ultimate shield against reactive behavior. It is the discipline to absorb an insult, a failure, or a tragedy without an immediate outburst of anger or despair. It is about internalizing the "heat" of an emotion and transforming it into quiet strength.

Psychological Mechanics: The "Gap"

In modern psychological terms, Nintai can be viewed as the mastery of the Space between Stimulus and Response.

  • Stimulus: An event occurs (pain, frustration, boredom).
  • The Gap: Nintai lives here. It is the conscious decision to breathe and remain centered.
  • Response: A measured, intentional action rather than a reflexive reaction.

By expanding this gap, an individual moves from being a victim of their environment to being a master of their internal state.

Cultivating Nintai in Daily Life

To build Nintai, one must treat it like a muscle that requires progressive loading.

  1. Voluntary Discomfort: Choosing the difficult path occasionally—such as taking the stairs, finishing a cold shower, or sitting still without a phone—strengthens the "Nin" (the heart's resilience).
  2. The "Stillness" Practice: When a negative impulse arises (the urge to complain or quit), practice staying physically still for sixty seconds. Observe the "blade" of the impulse without letting it cut your "heart."
  3. Reframing Time: Viewing long-term goals not as a "wait," but as a period of "refinement." Nintai transforms waiting from a passive act into an active, disciplined choice.

Summary

Nintai is the silent strength of the Japanese spirit. It is not a sign of weakness or submission, but rather a sign of immense internal power. To possess Nintai is to be like the mountain: unaffected by the wind and rain, remaining tall and unmoving regardless of the season.

Nihilism

What it is?

Nihilism is a philosophical belief that life lacks inherent meaning, value, or purpose. It questions traditional beliefs, moral values, and truths—often rejecting religious, political, or social systems as baseless. There are various types of nihilism (moral, existential, metaphysical), but the core theme is skepticism toward meaning and absolute truth.

“God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.”
— Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science (1882)

Historical background

  • The term “nihilism” comes from the Latin nihil, meaning "nothing."
  • Roots can be traced to early skeptical philosophy (e.g., Pyrrhonism).
  • Popularized in the 19th century, especially in Russia, where it became a social and political label during revolutionary movements.
  • Friedrich Nietzsche is the most famous thinker associated with existential nihilism, though he did not advocate for it, but warned about its dangers in a post-religious world.
  • Influential in existentialism, absurdism, and postmodernism.

Characteristics

  • Rejection of objective meaning: Belief that life has no ultimate purpose or intrinsic value.
  • Moral relativism or moral skepticism: Denial of universal moral truths.
  • Distrust in authority and systems: Critique of religion, ideology, politics.
  • Focus on individual freedom and responsibility (in existential interpretations).
  • Often associated with despair, detachment, or liberation depending on the interpretation.

Types

Type

Description

Existential Nihilism

Life has no intrinsic meaning or value.

Moral Nihilism

No objective moral truths exist; all values are human constructions.

Epistemological Nihilism

No knowledge is truly possible; truth is subjective or unknowable.

Metaphysical Nihilism

Denial of concrete existence — reality itself might be an illusion.

Political Nihilism

Rejection of political institutions and systems of power.

Core values

Unlike other philosophies, nihilism does not prescribe values — it often deconstructs them.

However, in response to nihilism, some thinkers propose new values or frameworks:

Theme

Implication

Meaninglessness

No predefined meaning in life → freedom or despair.

Freedom

Liberation from imposed values → possibility of self-created meaning.

Truth skepticism

Traditional truths are constructs → search for personal or pragmatic truth.

Benefits

  • Liberation from dogma: Enables critical thinking and questioning of inherited values.
  • Philosophical clarity: Forces confrontation with life’s uncertainties and illusions.
  • Freedom of self-definition: Opens the path to create your own meaning (existentialism).
  • Disruption of oppressive systems: Challenges political or religious institutions that rely on "absolute" truths.

Drawbacks or risks

  • Despair and hopelessness: Can lead to apathy or depression when life is seen as meaningless.
  • Moral collapse: Without a foundation of values, ethical guidance may erode.
  • Social alienation: Nihilistic views may conflict with societal norms and relationships.
  • Paralysis by meaninglessness: Risk of stagnation and loss of motivation.

For who

Best suited for…

Less suited for…

Philosophers, thinkers, skeptics

Those needing structure, faith, or optimism

People deconstructing ideology or dogma

Emotionally fragile or existentially anxious

Artists and postmodern writers

Those uncomfortable with ambiguity

Individuals seeking radical autonomy

Those looking for traditional moral grounding

Practical responses

While nihilism itself is deconstructive, many thinkers have offered constructive reactions:

Reaction

Thinker

Key Idea

Existentialism

Jean-Paul Sartre, Camus

Life is meaningless — but we can create our own meaning.

Absurdism

Albert Camus

We must embrace the absurd and live in defiance of it.

Transvaluation

Friedrich Nietzsche

Replace outdated values with new, life-affirming ones.

Pragmatism

William James

Truth is what works in practice — value lies in action.


Existentialism

What it is?

Existentialism is a philosophical movement centered on individual freedom, authenticity, and the search for meaning in a seemingly indifferent or meaningless universe. It emphasizes personal responsibility for giving life meaning through choices, actions, and self-definition, rather than relying on external systems like religion, culture, or tradition.

“Man is nothing else but what he makes of himself.”
— Jean-Paul Sartre


“The meaning of life is whatever you ascribe it to be.”
— Joseph Campbell

Historical background

  • Origins: Emerged in the 19th century as a response to the rise of rationalism, industrialization, and religious decline.
  • Precursors: Søren Kierkegaard (Christian existentialist) and Friedrich Nietzsche (atheistic existentialist).

  • Gained momentum in the 20th century through thinkers such as:

    • Jean-Paul Sartre – radical freedom, “existence precedes essence.”
    • Simone de Beauvoir – feminist existentialism and ethics.
    • Albert Camus – absurdism and rebellion.
    • Martin Heidegger – being and authenticity (Dasein).
  • Influenced literature, art, psychology, theology, and politics.

Core characteristics

  • Existence precedes essence: We are not born with a predefined purpose; we must create our own.
  • Radical freedom: We are free to choose, and thus responsible for who we become.
  • Authenticity: Living in alignment with one's true self rather than conforming.
  • Anxiety & dread (angst): Emotional response to freedom and the weight of responsibility.
  • Absurdity: The universe is indifferent, yet we long for meaning.

Core values

Value

Description

Freedom

The individual is free to choose and define their life.

Responsibility

With freedom comes full accountability for one’s actions.

Authenticity

Living true to one’s self, not to societal expectations.

Courage

Facing anxiety, absurdity, and isolation with resolve.

Self-awareness

Reflecting on existence and purpose with honesty.

Meaning-making

Creating one’s own meaning through choice, art, action, or relationships.

Key concepts

Concept

Meaning

Angst

A deep anxiety about freedom and responsibility.

Bad faith

Denying freedom by blaming circumstance, acting inauthentically.

The Absurd

The clash between the human desire for meaning and the universe’s silence.

Revolt

Choosing to live meaningfully despite absurdity (Camus).

Dasein

Heidegger’s concept of “being-there”—human consciousness in the world.

Benefits

  • Encourages deep self-reflection and growth.
  • Promotes personal freedom and autonomy.
  • Helps navigate crises of meaning or purpose.
  • Strengthens resilience in facing uncertainty, death, and suffering.
  • Fosters authentic relationships and intentional living.

Drawbacks or challenges

  • Can lead to existential anxiety, dread, or paralysis by overanalysis.
  • May be perceived as individualistic or nihilistic if misunderstood.
  • Not all individuals are comfortable with radical freedom and lack of external guidance.
  • Can feel burdensome due to its emphasis on responsibility and self-definition.

For who

Existentialism benefits:

  • Thinkers, seekers, and creatives questioning life’s meaning.
  • Individuals facing crises (loss, trauma, transitions).
  • Those who value personal autonomy and authenticity.
  • Anyone drawn to philosophical self-development and depth psychology.
  • Professionals in therapy, literature, art, and ethics.

Practical applications

  • Reflect on: “Who am I when no one is watching?”
  • Journal your thoughts on freedom, responsibility, and authenticity.
  • Read works like Nausea (Sartre), The Stranger (Camus), or The Sickness Unto Death (Kierkegaard).
  • Practice making meaningful choices aligned with your values, even when uncertain.
  • Accept existential anxiety as part of the human condition and a sign of freedom.


Absurdism

What it is?

Absurdism is a philosophical perspective that explores the conflict between the human desire for meaning and the silent, indifferent nature of the universe. It asserts that while life is inherently absurd (lacking clear purpose or reason), individuals must learn to live with this contradiction rather than deny or escape it.

“The absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.”
— Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus

Historical background

  • Origins: Rooted in existentialism and influenced by nihilism, Absurdism developed as a distinct philosophy in the 20th century, particularly during the post-war era.

  • Main figure: Albert Camus, French-Algerian philosopher, novelist, and essayist.

    • In The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), Camus presents the image of Sisyphus, condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, as a metaphor for human existence.
  • Closely related to existentialists like Sartre and Kierkegaard, though Camus rejected both religious hope and existential freedom as solutions to absurdity.

Core characteristics

  • The Absurd: The central theme—humans crave meaning, yet the universe offers none.
  • Conscious rebellion: Living fully in the face of absurdity, without resorting to false hope or escape.
  • Rejection of suicide and illusion: Camus called suicide a "confession" that life is not worth living. Instead, we must accept and confront the absurd.
  • Freedom through awareness: Awareness of absurdity frees the individual to live authentically and creatively.

Core values

Value

Description

Lucid awareness

Seeing life clearly, without illusions or false comfort.

Defiance

Living courageously despite the absurd.

Freedom

No external meaning → radical personal freedom to live as one chooses.

Joy in the moment

Finding fulfillment in experience itself, not in outcomes.

Integrity

Rejecting escapism (religion, nihilism, suicide) to live honestly.

Possible responses

  1. Suicide – Escaping the absurd by ending life (Camus rejects this as philosophical surrender).
  2. Philosophical Leap (Faith) – Believing in God or an external meaning (also rejected by Camus).
  3. Revolt – Accepting absurdity and continuing to live with passion and integrity.
“The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
— Camus

Benefits

  • Encourages radical honesty and rejection of comforting illusions.
  • Builds emotional resilience by facing life's difficulties without denial.
  • Liberates individuals to live authentically and passionately.
  • Promotes joy through experience, not external validation.
  • Encourages creative expression and existential courage.

Drawbacks or Challenges

  • Confronting absurdity can lead to existential dread, anxiety, or depression.
  • May be misunderstood as pessimistic or meaningless living.
  • Rejection of external systems (e.g., religion, ideology) may isolate some individuals.
  • Requires intellectual and emotional maturity to integrate fully.

For who

Absurdism benefits:

  • Individuals disillusioned by traditional belief systems.
  • People facing existential crises or profound life transitions.
  • Thinkers, artists, and writers who explore the human condition.
  • Anyone comfortable embracing paradox and contradiction.

Practical applications

  • Practice lucid awareness: Reflect on life's absurdities without rushing to fix them.
  • Read The Myth of Sisyphus, The Stranger, and The Plague by Camus.
  • Focus on the present moment and find joy in experience itself.
  • Create art, write, build, explore — not because it has "meaning," but because you're alive.
  • Develop a personal philosophy that embraces ambiguity, creativity, and rebellion.


Laws and rules

Laws

Parkinson law

Parkinson's law is the tendency for the amount of work required for something to increase so that it consumes any amount of time that may be allotted to it. The concept is often generalized to refer to the tendency for any available capacity in a given system to be used.

The implication is that no matter how extensive your resources, the demands on them will grow to ensure they're depleted. Parkinson's law has implications for many areas of business, including project management, time management, resource allocation, storage capacity planning and requirements analysis.


Murphy's law

Murphy's law is an adage or epigram that is typically stated as: "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong." In some formulations, it is extended to "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong, and at the worst possible time."


Hofstadter's law

Hofstadter's law is a self-referential adage, coined by Douglas Hofstadter in his book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979) to describe the widely experienced difficulty of accurately estimating the time it will take to complete tasks of substantial complexity:

Hofstadter's Law: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.

The law is often cited by programmers in discussions of techniques to improve productivity, such as The Mythical Man-Month or extreme programming.


Segal's law

Segal's law is an adage that states:

A man with a watch knows what time it is. A man with two watches is never sure.

The mood of the saying is ironic. While at a surface level it appears to be advocating the simplicity and self-consistency obtained by relying on information from only a single source, the underlying message is to gently question and make fun of such apparent certainty – a man with one watch can't really be sure he knows the right time, he merely has no way to identify error or uncertainty.

Nevertheless, the saying is also used in its purely surface sense, to caution against the potential pitfalls of having too much potentially conflicting information when making a decision.


Kidlin’s Law

Kidlin's Law states that, “If you can write the problem down then the matter is half solved.”


Gilbert’s Law

The biggest problem at work is that no one tells you what to do.


Walson’s Law

If you put information and intelligence first at all times. Then the money keeps coming in.


Falkland’s Law

When you don’t have to make a decision, then don’t make the decision.


Shelford's Law of Tolerance

PL: Prawo tolerancji Shelforda

Shelford's law of tolerance is a principle developed by American zoologist Victor Ernest Shelford in 1911. It states that an organism's success is based on a complex set of conditions and that each organism has a certain minimum, maximum, and optimum environmental factor or combination of factors that determine success.


Liebig's law of the minimum

PL: Prawo minimum Liebig'a

Liebig's law of the minimum, often simply called Liebig's law or the law of the minimum, is a principle developed in agricultural science by Carl Sprengel (1840) and later popularized by Justus von Liebig. It states that growth is dictated not by total resources available, but by the scarcest resource (limiting factor). The law has also been applied to biological populations and ecosystem models for factors such as sunlight or mineral nutrients. Liebig’s Law of the Minimum was formulated by German scientist Justus von Liebig. It states that if one essential plant nutrient is deficient, plant growth will be poor even when all other essential nutrients are abundant. Liebig’s Law of the Minimum is the scientific underpinning for the Liebig’s Barrel visualization below. Each stave of the barrel represents a different, essential nutrient. The length of each stave equals the amount of each nutrient in the soil available for plant uptake. If the limiting factor isn’t remedied, then your stave stays shorter and prevents your barrel from holding more water. The barrel shows just how important every nutrient is for a plant’s potential yield.

Benford's law

Benford's law, also known as the Newcomb–Benford law, the law of anomalous numbers, or the first-digit law, is an observation that in many real-life sets of numerical data, the leading digit is likely to be small. In sets that obey the law, the number 1 appears as the leading significant digit about 30% of the time, while 9 appears as the leading significant digit less than 5% of the time. If the digits were distributed uniformly, they would each occur about 11.1% of the time. Benford's law also makes predictions about the distribution of second digits, third digits, digit combinations, and so on.


Nie wszystkie duże, naturalne (niezmanipulowane) zbiory danych podlegają Prawu Benforda. Można wymienić kilka warunków koniecznych, które muszą być spełnione, aby wynik obserwacji był wiarygodny:

 

  1. Dane muszą być zgromadzone w tej samej przestrzeni fizycznej. Co za tym idzie dane muszą opisywać ten sam faktyczny stan rzeczy. Przykładem mogą być ceny oraz ilości, które nie powinny być uwzględniane w tym samym zestawie danych.
  2. Zbiór danych nie może posiadać górnej ani dolnej granicy przyjmowanych wartości. W szczególności oznacza to, że nie może istnieć limit determinujący to, czy poszczególna dana może być rozpatrywana w kontekście danego zbioru, czy też nie. Na przykład nie można rozpatrywać rachunku, gdzie księgowane są jedynie kwoty powyżej €400, a niższe księgowane na innym.
  3. Zbiór danych nie może posiadać żadnych przypisanych numerów. Służą one jedynie do identyfikacji i nie są wynikiem naturalnych procesów. Numery pracowników, numery kont bankowych, numery telefonów nie podlegają Prawu Benforda.
  4. Zestaw danych powinien posiadać więcej liczb o niższej wartości, niż wyższej. Jest to efekt naturalnego procesu rozwoju. Przykładowo można oczekiwać większej ilości faktur wystawionych na niższą kwotę, niż tych opiewających na pokaźne kwoty. Niemniej jednak zestaw danych nie musi być bardzo rozproszony.

 

W przypadku, gdy został utworzony Zbiór Benforda, można zaobserwować trzy główne cechy charakterystyczne:


  1. Niezmienność skali – mnożąc wszystkie wartości w Zbiorze Benforda przez stałą otrzymujemy inny, nowy Zbiór Benforda. Cecha ta jest szczególnie istotna w odniesieniu do przeliczania kursów walut.
  2. Niezmienność bazy – Theodore P. Hill (1995) udowodnił, że Prawo Benforda dotyczy nie tylko zbiorów opartych na dziesiętnym systemie liczbowym, ale również wszystkich innych systemach.
  3. Niezmienność w operacjach matematycznych – potęgowanie, mnożenie, dzielenie, dodawanie oraz odejmowanie Zbiorów Benforda ze sobą powoduje powstanie nowego Zbioru Benforda.


Applications

  • Accounting fraud detection - in 1972, Hal Varian suggested that the law could be used to detect possible fraud in lists of socio-economic data submitted in support of public planning decisions. Based on the plausible assumption that people who fabricate figures tend to distribute their digits fairly uniformly, a simple comparison of first-digit frequency distribution from the data with the expected distribution according to Benford's law ought to show up any anomalous results.
  • Use in criminal trials - in the United States, evidence based on Benford's law has been admitted in criminal cases at the federal, state, and local levels.
  • Election data - Such analysis is considered a simple, though not foolproof, method of identifying irregularities in election results. Scientific consensus to support the applicability of Benford's law to elections has not been reached in the literature.
  • Macroeconomic data - similarly, the macroeconomic data the Greek government reported to the European Union before entering the eurozone was shown to be probably fraudulent using Benford's law, albeit years after the country joined.
  • Price digit analysis - Benford's law as a benchmark for the investigation of price digits has been successfully introduced into the context of pricing research. The importance of this benchmark for detecting irregularities in prices was first demonstrated in a Europe-wide study which investigated consumer price digits before and after the euro introduction for price adjustments.
  • Genome data - The number of open reading frames and their relationship to genome size differs between eukaryotes and prokaryotes with the former showing a log-linear relationship and the latter a linear relationship. Benford's law has been used to test this observation with an excellent fit to the data in both cases.
  • Scientific fraud detection - A test of regression coefficients in published papers showed agreement with Benford's law. As a comparison group subjects were asked to fabricate statistical estimates. The fabricated results conformed to Benford's law on first digits, but failed to obey Benford's law on second digits.

Hofstadter's law

Hofstadter's law states that a project always takes longer than expected, even when the law is taken into account. Simply put, time estimates for how long a project will take to complete always fall short of the actual time required to complete it.


The law holds true even when the time allotment is increased to compensate for the human tendency toward underestimation. In other words, the law still proves true even when you factor in the possibility that you may need more time to complete the project.


Hofstadter's law is frequently evoked in the context of IT and software development. It is particularly relevant to time management, productivity, project management and DevOps.

Effects

Dunning–Kruger effect

PL: Efekt Dunninga-Krugera

The Dunning–Kruger effect is a cognitive bias whereby people with low ability, expertise, or experience regarding a certain type of task or area of knowledge tend to overestimate their ability or knowledge. Some researchers also include in their definition the opposite effect for high performers: their tendency to underestimate their skills.


Pygmalion effect

The Pygmalion effect, or Rosenthal effect, is a psychological phenomenon in which high expectations lead to improved performance in a given area. The effect is named for the Greek myth of Pygmalion, the sculptor who fell so much in love with the perfectly beautiful statue he created that the statue came to life. Leader expectations of an employee may alter leader behavior. The behavior a leader directs at an employee can affect employee behavior consistent with the leader's expectations.For example, a leader may expect an employee to be engaged in learning activities. In turn, the employee may engage in more learning, consistent with the idea self-fulfilling prophesy. Of course, leaders have power over employees (including the power to fire an employee) and, thus, behavior change in employees may be the result of that power differential.


Golem effect

The Golem effect is a psychological phenomenon in which lower expectations placed upon individuals either by supervisors or the individual themselves lead to poorer performance by the individual. This effect is mostly seen and studied in educational and organizational environments. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.


Matthew effect

The Matthew effect of accumulated advantage, Matthew principle, or Matthew effect for short, is sometimes summarized by the adage "the rich get richer and the poor get poorer". The concept is applicable to matters of fame or status, but may also be applied literally to cumulative advantage of economic capital. In the beginning, Matthew effects were primarily focused on the inequality in the way scientists were recognized for their work. However, Norman W. Storer, of Columbia University, led a new wave of research. He believed he discovered that the inequality that existed in the social sciences also existed in other institutions.


Hindsight bias

PL: Efekt pewności wstecznej

Hindsight bias, also known as the knew-it-all-along phenomenon or creeping determinism, is the common tendency for people to perceive past events as having been more predictable than they actually were.People often believe that after an event has occurred, they would have predicted or perhaps even would have known with a high degree of certainty what the outcome of the event would have been before the event occurred. Hindsight bias may cause distortions of memories of what was known or believed before an event occurred, and is a significant source of overconfidence regarding an individual's ability to predict the outcomes of future events.Examples of hindsight bias can be seen in the writings of historians describing outcomes of battles, physicians recalling clinical trials, and in judicial systems as individuals attribute responsibility on the basis of the supposed predictability of accidents.


Self-fulfilling prophecy

A self-fulfilling prophecy is the psychological phenomenon of someone "predicting" or expecting something, and this "prediction" or expectation coming true simply because the person believes or anticipates it will and the person's resulting behaviors align to fulfill the belief. This suggests that people's beliefs influence their actions. The principle behind this phenomenon is that people create consequences regarding people or events, based on previous knowledge of the subject.

There are three factors within an environment that can come together to influence the likelihood of a self-fulfilling prophecy becoming a reality: appearance, perception and belief. When a phenomenon cannot be seen, appearance is what we rely upon when a self-fulfilling prophecy is in place. When it comes to a self-fulfilling prophecy there also must be a distinction "between 'brute and institutional' facts".The philosopher John Searle states the difference as "facts [that] exist independently of any human institutions; institutional facts can only exist within institutions." There is an inability of institutional facts to be self-fulfilling. For example, the old belief that the Earth is flat (institutional) when it is known to be spherical (brute) is not self-fulfilling, because Earth's shape is proven through significant evidence. There has to be a consensus by "large numbers of people within a given population" —aside from being institutional, social, or bound by the laws of nature for an idea—to be seen as self-fulfilling.


Defensive design

Defensive design is the practice of planning for contingencies in the design stage of a project or undertaking. Essentially, it is the practice of anticipating all possible ways that an end-user could misuse a device, and designing the device so as to make such misuse impossible, or to minimize the negative consequences. For example, if it is important that a plug is inserted into a socket in a particular orientation, the socket and plug should be designed so that it is physically impossible to insert the plug incorrectly. Power sockets are often keyed in such a manner, to prevent the transposition of live and neutral. They are also recessed in the wall in a way that makes it impossible to touch connectors once they become live.


Rules

Hanlon's razor rule

PL: Brzytwa Hanlona

Hanlon's razor is an adage or rule of thumb that states "never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity." Known in several other forms, it is a philosophical razor that suggests a way of eliminating unlikely explanations for human behavior.


The 40% Rule

PL: Zasada 40%

he 40% Rule is the idea that when our mind is telling us to quit, that our body has actually only used up 40% of it’s potential. Think of this in terms of a workout; how many times have we been deep in a long grinder and that doubt begins to creep into the back of our head? Our mind begins to tell us to slow down or that it’s time to stop. According to the SEAL, at this point we are only 40% used up – and we are still capable of more. He explained that this extra 60% doesn’t come from the mind or from the body; it comes from our will.

Princpiles

Pareto principle

PL: Zasada Pareto

The Pareto principle states that for many outcomes, roughly 80% of consequences come from 20% of causes (the "vital few"). Other names for this principle are the 80/20 rule, the law of the vital few, or the principle of factor sparsity.

Management consultant Joseph M. Juran developed the concept in the context of quality control and improvement after reading the works of Italian sociologist and economist Vilfredo Pareto, who wrote about the 80/20 connection while teaching at the University of Lausanne. In his first work, Cours d'économie politique, Pareto showed that approximately 80% of the land in the Kingdom of Italy was owned by 20% of the population. The Pareto principle is only tangentially related to the Pareto efficiency.

Mathematically, the 80/20 rule is roughly described by a power law distribution (also known as a Pareto distribution) for a particular set of parameters. Many natural phenomena distribute according to power law statistics. It is an adage of business management that "80% of sales come from 20% of clients".
