Showing confidence

The key elements of demonstrating confidence, as discussed by Joe Navarro, center around the importance of non-verbal communication, preparation, and mindset. Below is a summary of the most important aspects:

Non-Verbal Communication and Body Language

  • Posture and Movement: Confidence is conveyed through posture, such as standing tall, keeping the chin up, and making deliberate, smooth gestures. Confident individuals move with purpose, whether walking to a podium, shaking hands, or simply taking a seat.
  • Eye Contact: Maintaining eye contact is crucial. Those who are less confident tend to avoid eye contact or glance around nervously, whereas confident individuals maintain steady, comfortable eye contact.
  • Gestures: Confident gestures are loose and controlled. For example, using a broader hand spread when making points or "steepling" the fingers can project authority and self-assurance. Conversely, fidgeting or jittery movements can undermine the perception of confidence.

Temporal Control and Cadence

  • Control of Time: Confident people take their time, whether walking, responding to questions, or delivering a speech. They are in charge of the pace of interactions, which demonstrates control and poise. This is contrasted with those who rush or feel pressured to respond quickly, often a sign of nervousness or insecurity.
  • Speech Cadence: The way one speaks can greatly influence how confidence is perceived. Speaking in a controlled cadence with deliberate pauses, as exemplified by leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. and Winston Churchill, holds the audience's attention and conveys authority. Avoiding "up talk," where statements end with a questioning tone, is essential to projecting confidence.

Modeling Confidence

  • Socialization and Role Models: Confidence can be learned by observing and modeling the behavior of high-status individuals or public figures. This might include adopting their posture, speech patterns, or even their way of dressing. For example, Joe Navarro mentions Cary Grant, who deliberately adopted the behaviors of high-status individuals to shape his confident persona.
  • Practice and Rehearsal: Confidence in public speaking or any other form of presentation often comes from thorough preparation and rehearsal. Practicing speeches, refining gestures, and even doing physical warm-ups, like leaning into a wall to release tension, can help reduce anxiety and project confidence.

Psychological Aspects and Self-Perception

  • Internal Mindset: Confidence starts from within. Recognizing that it is natural to feel nervous, especially in public speaking, allows one to address those feelings constructively. Building confidence involves knowing the material thoroughly, which in turn reduces anxiety and enhances the ability to project assurance.
  • Focus on Mastery: Confidence is not inherent but developed through mastery of skills, knowledge, and self-presentation. Whether it's a professional task, a public performance, or even a social interaction, the more prepared and skilled a person is, the more naturally confident they will appear.
  • Authenticity vs. Theatricality: True confidence is often quiet and self-assured rather than loud or ostentatious. It’s about being in control of oneself and one’s environment, rather than relying on exaggerated displays of power or dominance.

Practical Tips for Building Confidence

  • Be Honest: Acknowledge that feeling nervous is normal and use that awareness to prepare more effectively.
  • Prepare Thoroughly: Confidence is directly tied to preparation. Knowing your material inside and out makes you more secure and reduces the fear of being caught off guard.
  • Rehearse: Rehearsing your delivery helps you feel more comfortable and familiar with the material, reducing anxiety when the time comes to present or speak.
  • Physical Warm-ups: Simple physical exercises before a presentation can help alleviate nervousness and make you feel more powerful and ready to take control of the stage.

Confidence as a Growth Process

  • Developing Confidence Over Time: Confidence can be nurtured at any stage of life, regardless of background or physical ability. It is cultivated through achievements, pushing boundaries, and continuously working on self-improvement. It’s a skill that grows with experience, practice, and self-awareness.

By focusing on these elements—non-verbal cues, temporal control, social modeling, preparation, and mindset—anyone can learn to project confidence effectively, whether in personal interactions, professional settings, or public speaking.


Detect lying & deception

Detecting deception is a complex process that involves observing a range of behaviors and responses, rather than relying on a single, universal indicator. While common myths suggest that gaze aversion, fidgeting, or grooming gestures like touching one's hair or clothes automatically indicate lying, these are not definitive signs on their own. Instead, deception detection requires a holistic approach, considering various physiological, cognitive, and behavioral cues.

Key Components of Deception Detection:

  1. Fight-or-Flight Response:

    • When people lie, they often experience stress, triggering the fight-or-flight response. This response can manifest as physiological changes like a dry mouth (leading to deep swallowing), increased heart rate, or fidgeting. For instance, Jodi Arias, during her interrogation, displayed an extreme example of this by performing a handstand, indicating a need to release nervous energy.

  2. Cognitive Complexity:

    • Liars tend to keep their stories simple, often focusing only on what they saw or heard. They might avoid details involving other senses or complex spatial and relational aspects. When questioned about specifics or asked to recount the same event in different ways, their stories often fall apart. This method of probing deeper into a story’s complexity can reveal inconsistencies, exposing the deception.

  3. Perception Management:

    • Some individuals attempt to manage how they are perceived during an interview by behaving in a way they believe is expected of a truthful person. For example, a liar might suddenly stop fidgeting, trying to appear calm and collected. However, this change in behavior, especially if it contrasts with their earlier demeanor, can be a red flag.

  4. Misinterpretation of Stress Indicators:

    • The story of the woman at the FBI office illustrates how stress-related behaviors (e.g., biting her lip, touching her neck, fidgeting) can be easily misinterpreted as indicators of deception. In reality, her anxiety stemmed from a completely unrelated concern—her parking meter running out. This example highlights that behaviors often thought to be signs of lying may simply indicate psychological discomfort due to various reasons unrelated to deception.

  5. Psychological Discomfort vs. Deception:

    • The speaker argues that behaviors indicating psychological discomfort, such as touching the face or fidgeting, do not necessarily point to lying. Instead, these behaviors reflect stress or anxiety, which can be caused by numerous factors, including fear of authority, nervousness about being in a high-stakes situation, or even minor concerns like the parking meter example. Thus, it is crucial not to assume these behaviors are signs of deception.

  6. The Importance of Creating a Comfortable Environment:

    • The speaker stresses the importance of creating a relaxed environment during interviews. Techniques such as maintaining a calm tone, giving the interviewee space, and avoiding direct eye contact help reduce stress, leading to better recall and more accurate information. Creating psychological pressure, on the other hand, can hinder the interview process and lead to unreliable outcomes.

  7. Challenges of Traditional Deception Indicators:

    • The speaker debunks long-held beliefs about traditional indicators of deception, such as touching the nose or mouth, or looking in certain directions when answering questions. These so-called indicators have no scientific basis and can lead to false conclusions, as they were taught and believed for decades without evidence to support their accuracy.

  8. The Dangers of Misinterpreting Behaviors:

    • The speaker discusses the serious consequences of misinterpreting behaviors as deception. For example, in cases of wrongful convictions, DNA exonerations have shown that those who were believed to be lying were actually telling the truth. Moreover, about 25% of wrongfully convicted individuals admitted to crimes they didn't commit simply to end the intense psychological pressure during interrogations.

  9. The Limits of Nonverbal Cues in Court:

    • Nonverbal behaviors are not admissible as evidence in court because they are subjective and open to interpretation. The speaker gives an example where a suspect’s reaction to a specific word (like "ice pick") was a clue to their guilt, but such nonverbal cues alone wouldn't hold up in court without additional evidence.

  10. The Prevalence and Acceptance of Lying:

    • Lying is presented as a common social behavior, often used for social survival. People lie for various reasons, from avoiding conflict to making others feel better. However, habitual liars, such as the spy described in the transcription, can be particularly difficult to detect because they are practiced and skilled in deception.

  11. Critical Thinking Over Assumptions:

    • The speaker emphasizes the need for critical thinking and verification when assessing the truthfulness of someone's statements. Rather than relying on nonverbal cues, it is more effective to cross-check the details of the story and observe if the narrative holds up under scrutiny. Cognitive load, or the difficulty someone has in answering simple questions, can be a more reliable indicator that something is off, though not necessarily proof of lying.

  12. The Myth of Deception Detection Expertise:

    • The speaker strongly cautions against claims of being able to detect deception based on body language alone. There is no scientific basis for such claims, and relying on them can lead to serious errors in judgment, including wrongful convictions and ruining lives.

Verbal and Nonverbal Indicators:

  1. Verbal Cues:

    • Liars often use hedging words like “sort of,” “almost,” or “kind of” to soften their statements, indicating a lack of confidence in what they are saying. For example, saying "I sort of did my homework" suggests that the task may not have been completed.

  2. Nonverbal Behavior:

    • Changes in posture, sudden movements, or grooming gestures during questioning can indicate deception. Observing these shifts, especially after establishing a baseline of normal behavior (norming), helps in identifying when someone might be lying.

  3. Non-Linguistic Verbal Cues:

    • Changes in speech patterns, such as an increase in the pace, volume, or pitch of speech, can signal stress and potential deception. For example, a higher pitch may indicate nervousness associated with lying.

Examples

  • Scott Peterson: During his interrogation about his missing wife, Laci, Peterson's behavior and speech provided clues to his deception. The investigator’s focus should have been more on observing these behaviors rather than merely taking notes, as writing can distract from picking up on critical nonverbal cues.
  • President Nixon: His infamous “I’m not a crook” speech showed verbal indicators of deception, such as unnecessary filler phrases and an increased pace in his speech, which suggested nervousness and a lack of confidence in his statement.
  • President Clinton: In denying his affair with Monica Lewinsky, Clinton used carefully chosen words, like referring to Lewinsky as “that woman” and denying “sexual relations,” which was an attempt to narrowly define his actions and avoid admitting guilt. This type of language manipulation is a classic example of a lie of omission.

The Importance of Holistic Analysis:

Deception detection is most effective when it takes into account the entire range of behaviors and responses from an individual. This means not only focusing on what is said but also how it is said, the physical behaviors that accompany the speech, and the broader context of the situation. A comprehensive analysis, combined with strategic questioning, can uncover inconsistencies and reveal the truth, even in the most deceptive individuals.

The transcription underscores the importance of not over-relying on nonverbal cues as indicators of deception. While behaviors can suggest psychological discomfort, they do not necessarily indicate lying. Effective deception detection requires a comprehensive approach, including careful questioning, verification of facts, and an understanding of the context behind behaviors. Ultimately, the speaker warns against the dangers of assuming expertise in deception detection, as this can have severe and far-reaching consequences.

Positive body language

Introduction

  • Positive body language refers to non-verbal cues—such as gestures, facial expressions and posture—that communicate how a person feels, often subconsciously.
  • Your body language can reinforce or contradict spoken words, so becoming aware of it can improve workplace communication.
  • Interpretations differ across cultures—what appears positive in one culture may seem neutral or negative in another.

Examples

  1. Eye Contact

    • Shows engagement, confidence and active listening, especially useful in interviews.
    • Cultural note: In some cultures, such as Māori and Samoan, prolonged eye contact may be seen as disrespectful.

  2. Head Nod

    • Signals understanding, agreement and encourages the speaker to continue.
    • Cultural note: In Bulgaria, nodding can sometimes indicate disagreement.

  3. Firm Handshake

    • Conveys confidence and respect; matching the other person’s grip works well.
    • Cultural note: A firm grip may be impolite in some regions (e.g., some Middle Eastern cultures); in Japan, a bow may replace a handshake.

  4. Open Palms

    • Suggests openness, honesty and receptiveness, making others feel more comfortable.

  5. Upright, Open Posture

    • Sitting or standing upright with open body posture (not crossing arms/legs) shows approachability, confidence and engagement.

  6. Leaning In

    • Slightly leaning forward demonstrates interest and attentiveness.
    • Cultural note: Personal-space expectations vary—what feels attentive in one culture may feel intrusive in another.

Importance

  • Reduces Misunderstandings: Improves clarity and comprehension, helping avoid miscommunication and workplace errors.
  • Supports a Professional Image: Reinforces your spoken message and helps you appear confident, honest and competent.
  • Boosts Team Spirit: Encourages morale, engagement and positive interaction. When demonstrated by one team member, others often mirror it.
  • Enhances Leadership Effectiveness: Leaders who use positive body language build trust, communicate clearly and motivate better.
  • Builds Rapport: Helps create stronger relationships and better cooperation through approachability and attentiveness.

Summary

  • Being aware of your own and others’ body language helps align non-verbal cues with your intended message.
  • Cultural awareness is essential—eye contact, gestures, distance and touch vary widely across cultures.
  • While valuable, body language shouldn’t overshadow evaluating skills and should accommodate diverse communication styles.


Taking/giving criticism

What it is?

Criticism is the construction of a judgement about the negative or positive qualities of someone or something. Criticism can range from impromptu comments to a written detailed response. Criticism falls into several overlapping types including "theoretical, practical, impressionistic, affective, prescriptive, or descriptive".


What is constructive criticism?

Constructive criticism focuses on providing constructive feedback, supported by specific examples, to help you improve in some area. Constructive criticism should be offered in a friendly manner with good intentions. Ideally, the person offering constructive criticism should also be prepared to help brainstorm possible solutions and next steps in order to serve as a valuable tool in the growth process.


It’s important to note that constructive criticism is not negative criticism, nor should it be interpreted that way. Though constructive criticism won’t always be positive, it should be centered around helping someone improve—not tearing them down.

Constructive criticism vs. destructive criticism

Constructive criticism

Constructive criticism is clear, direct, honest, and easy to implement. It provides specific examples and actionable suggestions for positive change. This type of feedback also highlights ways the recipient can make positive improvements in their behavior to minimize future problems.

Deconstructive criticism

Destructive criticism, on the other hand, focuses solely on the problem. This kind of feedback offers no encouragement, help, or support for improvement. Despite the deliverer’s intentions, it often lowers morale and reduces confidence.


Unlike constructive criticism, destructive criticism is feedback that isn’t designed to help you improve and grow into a better person, employee, or friend. Instead, destructive criticism is:

  • Intended as a personal attack
  • Formatted to harm someone’s self-esteem
  • Public
  • Not specific or actionable
  • Hypercritical or needlessly nit-picky


Benefits

Even if you give the perfect piece of advice, constructive criticism is still difficult to both give and receive. But don’t shy away from this type of feedback just because it’s difficult. In fact, constructive criticism can help both you and the person you’re giving feedback to grow—both personally and professionally.

Tips

Do: Use “I” statements

“I” statements are a way to express your opinion by focusing on the situation, rather than the person you’re talking about. “I” statements begin with “I feel…” or “I think…” instead of “You said…” or “You did…”


With an “I” statement, you can make feedback feel less personal by centering it around your experience. By beginning every sentence with “I,” you’re constantly clarifying that you’re sharing your thoughts and opinions—rather than objective fact. This can help reduce the feelings of personal defensiveness that often come with any kind of criticism, and make the entire feedback session more productive.

Don’t: Use the sandwich method

You’ve likely heard of the sandwich method (sometimes called the “feedback sandwich”) before—this is possibly the most well-known criticism strategy. In the sandwich method, you start off with a positive note, mention a constructive criticism, then finish off with another positive comment.

Despite its popularity, the sandwich method isn’t an effective way to communicate helpful, constructive criticism. Because you’re nesting the constructive criticism, there's little opportunity to make that feedback actionable or brianstorm next steps. Instead, spend your time making your feedback as specific and helpful as possible—no matter how many pieces of feedback you have to give.

Do: Provide actionable feedback

The goal of providing constructive feedback is to give the person something they can work on. In addition to pointing out what could be improved, good constructive criticism includes ideas and next steps that the person can take in order to further develop their skills. When you provide your feedback, make sure to clarify that you’re open to further discussion or brainstorming if that would be helpful for the person you’re giving feedback to.

If your feedback isn’t actionable, don’t give it, or wait until you have something actionable before bringing it to the person’s attention. Without actionable advice, your feedback strays dangerously close to destructive criticism, rather than constructive help.

Don’t: Publicly share your feedback

Even the best-phrased criticism can be hard to take, especially if the person you’re giving feedback to spent a lot of time and energy on their work. In order for feedback to be constructive and helpful, you want to open a dialogue about how the person can improve.

This type of dialogue isn’t possible if you share your feedback publicly. Instead of starting a conversation, the person might feel embarrassed, ashamed, or personally attacked. They might respond defensively or just move on without internalizing the feedback. Make sure you’re taking the time to sit down and chat, in order to have the most productive conversation. Either schedule time to give constructive criticism, or use a regularly scheduled 1:1 to do so.

Do: Include positive comments where appropriate

Just because the sandwich method isn’t the best way to provide feedback doesn’t mean you shouldn’t give positive feedback. Constructive criticism shouldn’t just be about negative feedback. Telling someone what they’ve done well is just as helpful. That way, they can spend time honing their strengths—in addition to strengthening their weaknesses.

Don’t: Force positivity

That being said, just like you want to avoid the sandwich method, you should also avoid forced positivity. The point of constructive feedback isn’t to give the person meaningless compliments—it’s to help them move forward and improve.

No matter what type of feedback you’re giving, make sure you think it through and really mean it. Insincere feedback can feel unhelpful and make future feedback sessions more difficult.

Do: Make it a conversation

Constructive criticism isn’t valuable unless there’s a give and take aspect. Part of using “I” statements is to provide feedback from your perspective. The person you’re giving feedback to, though, might have a different point of view. Give them time to ask questions about why you feel the way you do and how they can improve based on your feedback. Keep in mind that the best feedback is collaborative, not prescriptive.

Don’t: Attempt to “surprise” with feedback

Giving feedback can be uncomfortable. Sometimes, it might feel awkward or unpleasant to let the person know you want to give them some feedback—what if they come into the conversation on the defensive, or have additional questions for you?

Though feedback sessions can be uncomfortable, attempting to “surprise” someone with feedback can turn a potential growth moment into a negative experience. If your feedback comes from left field, it can be frustrating, overwhelming, and make the person feel personally attacked. Instead, make sure you let the person know that this will be a feedback session.

Do: Give feedback in a timely manner

Constructive criticism is helpful if it’s given relatively soon after the action occurred. That way, the scenario is fresh in both of your minds. If you wait too long, your feedback might be less relevant, which makes it less helpful. Aim to give feedback within 2-7 days of the situation.

Don’t: Give feedback without thinking it over

Even though you do want to give feedback in a timely manner, you don’t want to give it immediately without thought. Even if you had a lightbulb moment of realization of how this person could improve, wait at least a day to make sure this feedback needs to be expressed and that you can do so in a constructive, positive way. Before scheduling your feedback session, ask yourself:

  • Is this feedback something that will help them improve?
  • Do they need to hear this feedback?
  • Am I prepared to help them brainstorm how to improve?
  • What, if any, next steps can the person take?

Do: Maintain a friendly tone and body language

Ultimately, you’re providing feedback in order to help a person improve. Even if the feedback is hard to give, make sure you’re keeping your body language positive and your tone light.

You might not feel comfortable giving constructive criticism at first, so consider practicing what you’re going to say and how you’re going to say it. Pay particular attention to your tone, and make sure you aren’t frowning, glaring, or crossing your arms. Even if you aren’t actually frustrated, these signals can raise the person’s defensiveness and lead to an unproductive feedback session. If you’re giving feedback remotely, be sure to turn your video on for the call.

Don't: putting yourself in their shoes

You’ll often hear people recommend that you “put yourself in someone else’s shoes” to understand where they’re coming from. And it’s true that putting yourself in someone’s shoes is a great way to build emotional intelligence. 

However, avoid doing this when you’re offering feedback. Unfortunately, when we try to put ourselves in other people’s shoes while offering feedback, it often sounds like we know better than them. Remember: feedback is an opinion, not a fact. 

Phrases to avoid: 

  • “If I were you…” 
  • “You should have…” 
  • “When I’m in your shoes…” 

Receiving constructive criticism

Accepting constructive criticism without getting defensive can be really difficult. Even though you conceptually know the person is giving feedback to help you, it’s human nature to feel a little defensive when receiving criticism—even if it is helpful.


Even if you do receive unprompted constructive criticism, as long as it isn’t destructive criticism, try these six steps to become a pro at receiving criticism:

  1. Avoid immediately reacting. Feedback can engage our fight or flight response and turn a theoretically helpful session into an adrenaline-filled challenge. Before responding, take a deep breath and resist the urge to react, respond, or argue.
  2. If need be, remind yourself that constructive criticism can help you improve. Even if you didn’t know this feedback was coming, try to remember that this constructive criticism is being offered with your best interests at heart.
  3. Listen to understand—not to respond. When someone is offering constructive criticism, listen without formulating a reply or a defensive response to the feedback. Keep in mind that the person is offering feedback in order to try to help you, and try to listen with an open mind.
  4. Connect the feedback to your role, not to yourself. Feedback feels personal because we think people are criticizing us. But in a business setting, constructive criticism is usually based on your role. Good feedback can help you improve in your job and often isn’t as personal as it feels.
  5. Thank the person giving you feedback. Giving constructive feedback is hard. Thank the person for their energy and effort in helping you improve.
  6. Ask questions, but don’t challenge the feedback. Though you shouldn’t challenge or refute the feedback, it’s ok to ask questions and brainstorm how you can improve. If you aren’t ready to ask questions immediately after receiving critical feedback, that’s ok too. Set a follow up meeting to chat more about how you can improve.




Assertiveness


Styles


Aggressive


Getting feedback

Introduction

Receiving feedback well does not mean you must always accept it or act upon it. Rather, it means engaging in the conversation skillfully, managing emotional triggers, and making an informed choice about how to use the information provided.

Types

We often fail to benefit from feedback because we confuse its purpose. There are three distinct categories:

  • Appreciation: Designed to motivate, encourage, and acknowledge effort. It builds the "emotional bank account" of a relationship.
  • Coaching: Focused on helping someone expand their knowledge, sharpen a skill, or improve a trait.
  • Evaluation: Assessing a person against a set of standards or peers. It aligns expectations and informs decision-making (e.g., performance reviews).
The "Cross-Transaction" Trap: Problems arise when the receiver wants Appreciation, but the giver provides Coaching. If you feel discouraged after a meeting, ask yourself: "What kind of feedback was I looking for, and what did I actually get?"

Triggers

When we react defensively, it is usually because the feedback has hit one of three "triggers." Identifying which one is active can help you regain control.


Trigger Type

Focus

The Internal Reaction

Truth Triggers

The Substance

"That’s simply wrong/unfair/unhelpful."

Relationship Triggers

The Giver

"After all I've done for you? Who are you to tell me this?"

Identity Triggers

The Self

"I am a failure. I am not the person I thought I was."

Overcoming Truth Triggers

We often focus on what is wrong with the feedback to dismiss it. Instead, try to find what might be right.

  • Unpack Labels: Feedback like "Be more proactive" is a vague label. Ask: "What exactly do you see me doing (or not doing) that leads to that conclusion?"
  • Identify Blind Spots: We judge ourselves by our intentions, but others judge us by our behavior (body language, tone, impact). Accept that others see things about you that you literally cannot see.

Overcoming Relationship Triggers

Don't let the "who" drown out the "what." Avoid switchtracking—where one person talks about the feedback and the other talks about the relationship.

  • Example: "You're late with the report." -> "Well, you never gave me the data!" (Two different tracks).
  • Strategy: Acknowledge both tracks but discuss them separately.

System Perspective: It’s Not Just You

Feedback often implies "You are the problem." However, most issues are a result of the intersection between two people and their environment.

  • You + Me: Personal differences in work style or communication.
  • Role Clashes: The conflict may be inherent to your job titles (e.g., Sales vs. Compliance), not your personalities.
  • The Environment: Processes, physical space, or external pressures that contribute to the friction.

Role of Mindset and Personality

How we process feedback is deeply rooted in our "wiring" and our psychological narrative.

The "Second Score"

In every feedback situation, you are being evaluated twice. The First Score is the feedback itself (the critique of your work). The Second Score is how you handle the feedback. Even if the first score is bad, you can still "ace" the second score by remaining professional and curious.

Growth vs. Fixed Mindset

  • Fixed Mindset: Feedback is a verdict on your abilities. "If I'm not perfect, I'm a failure."
  • Growth Mindset: Feedback is information for evolution. Your identity is a "work in progress."

Baseline and Recovery

We all have a "Baseline" level of happiness. Negative feedback can cause a "swing" away from that baseline. Some people recover in minutes; others take days. Knowing your recovery profile helps you tell yourself: "I feel terrible right now, but I know I’ll feel better by tomorrow morning."

Strategies for Getting the Most Out of Feedback

To turn a potentially painful conversation into a growth opportunity, use these tactical approaches:

  1. The "One Thing" Question: Ask your manager or peer: "What is one thing you see me doing (or failing to do) that is getting in my own way?" This makes the feedback specific and manageable.
  2. Separate Feelings from Stories: We often create a "catastrophic story" (e.g., "I'm going to get fired") from a single piece of feedback. Stick to the facts.
  3. The 10-Year Test: Will this feedback matter in a decade? Usually, the answer is no. This provides immediate perspective.
  4. Use "And" instead of "But": When turning down feedback, say: "I hear your point, AND I have decided to prioritize this other task for now." This acknowledges the giver without being dismissive.

When to Reject Feedback

Not all feedback is worth taking. You should set boundaries if the feedback is:

  • Cruel or Abusive: Aimed at demeaning you rather than helping you.
  • Relentless: A "moving goalpost" where nothing is ever enough.
  • Held Hostage: Used as a threat to the stability of the relationship.

How to say no: "I appreciate you sharing that, but I’m not open to feedback on this topic right now." Being firm and appreciative is a sign of a high-functioning identity.

Posture

The Principles of Posture

When it comes to taking care of our bodies, our backs are one of the most important parts! This central space connects every part of you and provides the mobility you need to perform even the most basic of tasks. That’s why even the most minor of back injuries or spasms can have us bedridden for hours at a time. When it comes to the health of our backs, one of the best ways to prevent back pain is to consistently practice good posture.


There are five principles of posture and movement that outline the ways our bodies work:

  • Posture Principle 1 – Movement. Your body is designed to move and stay moving. Posture ensures that you can do this effectively
  • Posture Principle 2 – Balance. Proper posture allows you to balance your body against gravity comfortably and safely.
  • Posture Principle 3 – Movement Patterns. The pattern of your body’s motion goes down the easiest path. This prevents your body from straining.
  • Posture Principle 4 – Compensation. Your body learns patterns naturally to guide movement. When you experience pain, your body alters the way it moves in order to avoid pain.
  • Posture Principle 5 – Adaptation. When you change your posture and motion, your body’s physiology also changes.

Each healthy back has three curves that are considered to be best for posture, balance, and overall wellness:

  • Cervical curve: An inward or forward curve at your neck
  • Thoracic curve: The outward or backward curve at your upper back
  • Lumbar curve: The inward curve of your lower back.


There are three parts of your posture that determine how aligned and comfortable your body is:

  • Spine: Proper posture is all about keeping the curves of your spine aligned properly and balanced. When the disks in your spine are not properly placed, it can lead to abnormalities and pain.
  • Muscles: Strengthening the muscles in your abdominals, hips, and legs can help keep the muscles in your back strong enough to support the natural curves.
  • Joints: Your hips, knees, and ankles balance your back’s curves. This is what allows you to maintain proper posture no matter which way you move.

Eye contact

Introduction


Importance

Eye contact is an important part of communication. But in order to understand why, we must first answer an important question:

What does eye contact mean?

Eye contact is what happens when two people look at each other’s eyes at the same time. This is a form of nonverbal communication that humans use to communicate many forms of emotions.

Unlike other primates, we can easily see where humans are looking because of the amount of white surrounding our irises. As a result, we know where someone is looking even when their head doesn't move.

This is why eye contact plays a huge role in communication.

Let’s explore four reasons why eye contact communication is important:

Bond with others

Research has shown that eye contact activates the limbic mirror system. This means that the same neurons that are firing in someone’s brain will also fire in yours when you share eye contact with them.

So, if their eyes are communicating joy, neurons on your end will also fire to feel joy.

This sharing of emotional states can help you bond with others and increase empathy between individuals.

Display honesty

Good eye contact is an important display of honesty during a conversation.

The eyes are a central part of nonverbal communication. They show a range of emotions that words won’t always speak. And honesty can help two people build trust.

Increase your resistance to persuasion

Research has shown that direct eye contact can make you more resistant to persuasion and influence tactics. You can use this nonverbal cue to be more aware of other people’s influence over you.

Improve understanding between people

It’s easy to have misunderstandings, even when two people believe they’re both listening intently. Making eye contact helps both people focus on the conversation and read facial expressions. This can improve understanding.

And improving understanding can significantly improve communication between two people.

Build respect

Finally, making eye contact shows and earns respect.

Of course, it takes more than eye contact alone to nurture respect in a relationship. But it plays an important role. Looking someone in the eyes shows them that you think they are important.

Increases intimacy

Although the available research is old, there’s some evidence that long eye contact can increase intimacy.

In a pair of studies from 1989, strangers who looked into each other’s eyes for 2 minutes experienced mutual feelings of love. A 2003 studyTrusted Source found that the longer someone started at a face, the more they became attracted to it.

Must know

Eye contact helps others remember what you said

When you share eye contact during a conversation, you’ll remember more of what the other person said.

The reverse is true as well. Other people will retain more of what you said.

Research found that during a video call, participants retained more of the information from the call when there was more eye contact involved. And, people don’t even need a huge amount of eye contact to get this benefit.

The researchers found that a direct gaze for 30% of the interaction is all it takes for participants to significantly increase what they remembered from the call.

Eye contact can help with self-awareness

Being self-aware means that you are aware of what’s currently happening with your body. And eye contact can help with that, according to research from the University of Paris.

Their research found that people are more self-aware when they’re making effective eye contact than when they’re avoiding eye contact.

Researchers theorize that we’re more focused on our own bodies and behavior when other people look at us.

Eye contact creates attraction

Eye contact attraction is a real thing. Research shows that humans find other people more attractive when they make eye contact.

Smiling can also help create attraction.

While this is important for personal relationships, it also matters at work. Colleagues and leaders will be more inclined to build relationships with you when you look them in the eye.

On the other hand, no eye contact can show a lack of confidence.

Tips

If you find that your eyes wander away from the other person’s eyes during social interactions, or if you have social anxiety, here are five tips you can use to improve and make eye contact more often.  

Make eye contact before you start talking

Before you utter your first word, make eye contact. When the contact is established, you can start talking face-to-face.

Hold your gaze for 4 to 5 seconds at a time

Not sure how long you should hold another person’s gaze or how much eye contact to make? Try looking into people’s eyes for four to five seconds at a time.

Instead of looking down when you break eye contact, look to the side. Then, you can resume eye contact.

Use gestures

Do you ever feel uncomfortable and want to break eye contact? Instead of just looking away, try using gestures and body language.

You can nod, use your hands, or use other gestures that you usually make during a conversation.

This will look more natural than just looking away.

Move your eyes slowly

Avoid looking away too quickly when you break eye contact. This can make you seem nervous.

Instead, look away slowly.

Maintain eye contact 50% of the time

When you’re having a discussion with someone, use the 50/70 rule. This means you should hold eye contact between 50%–70% of the time.

Maintain this amount of eye contact both while you are talking and while you are listening.








Antifragile ego

What it is?

An antifragile ego is a self-concept that becomes stronger, more adaptive, and more self-aware through criticism, setbacks, and challenges.

It’s based on the concept of antifragility introduced by Nassim Nicholas Taleb (2012):

“The fragile breaks under pressure, the robust resists it, but the antifragile grows from it.”

Applied to psychology:

  • A fragile ego shatters when criticized.
  • A robust ego endures criticism but learns little from it.
  • An antifragile ego uses criticism and failure as fuel for growth, refinement, and deeper self-knowledge.

Origin of the concept

Taleb’s Framework (2012)

In Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder, Taleb describes systems that benefit from stressors and volatility.

They don’t just survive uncertainty — they evolve through it.

The Power Moves Interpretation

The Power Moves article extends this to personal psychology, arguing that people can develop an “antifragile ego” — a self that doesn’t rely on external validation or status, and instead grows stronger under social pressure, failure, or rejection.

Psychological Foundation

The antifragile ego draws from:

  • Resilience theory (Bonanno, 2004): psychological flexibility after adversity.
  • Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000): intrinsic self-worth independent of external approval.
  • Ego development theory (Loevinger, 1976): maturity through integration of contradictions and complexity.

Understanding the ego

Functional Role of the Ego

In psychoanalytic and modern terms, the ego is the self-regulatory and identity-maintaining structure of the psyche.

It mediates between:

  • The id (instincts, impulses),
  • The superego (ideals, conscience),
  • The external world (feedback, reality).

A healthy ego maintains coherence (sense of “I”) while integrating feedback and change.

Fragile vs. Antifragile Ego Dynamics


Type

Definition

Reaction to Feedback

Fragile Ego

Dependent on validation and appearances.

Collapses or retaliates when criticized.

Robust Ego

Stable, self-assured.

Resists stress but doesn’t necessarily grow.

Antifragile Ego

Open, self-updating identity.

Learns, adapts, and strengthens under challenge.

The antifragile ego thrives on stressors of self-perception — it welcomes being proven wrong because each correction increases its accuracy.

Core characteristics


Dimension

Description

Self-honesty

The ability to look at one’s flaws and mistakes without denial.

Low dependence on external validation

Self-worth is intrinsic and self-generated.

Growth orientation

Failure and criticism are used as feedback for learning.

Ego flexibility

Identity is not rigid; it updates with new information.

Humility and curiosity

Acknowledging limits of knowledge; curiosity replaces defensiveness.

Self-distancing

Ability to observe one’s ego from a meta-perspective (metacognition).

Emotional regulation

Managing shame, embarrassment, and anger productively.

Resilience + Antifragility

Bounces back and improves after ego threats.

Psychological mechanisms

Cognitive Reframing

Antifragile individuals reinterpret ego threats not as attacks, but as data.

“Criticism isn’t humiliation — it’s free information about how I’m perceived.”

This mindset shifts pain into feedback, fostering cognitive and emotional growth.

Self-Complexity

According to Linville (1985), individuals with multiple self-aspects (roles, values, identities) experience less psychological damage from ego threats.

Antifragile egos maintain diversity in identity — so a failure in one domain doesn’t destroy self-worth.

Neurobiological Correlates

  • Prefrontal cortex: mediates reflection and emotional regulation.
  • Anterior cingulate cortex (ACC): detects conflicts and errors; learning signal.
  • Amygdala downregulation via mindfulness and self-distancing enhances composure during ego stress.

Transformation path: from fragile to antifragile ego


Stage

Description

Typical Behaviors

Fragile

Dependent on approval; overreacts to threats.

Defensiveness, denial, blame-shifting.

Robust

Stable identity; tolerates feedback.

Calm, but resistant to change.

Adaptive

Begins using failure as a guide.

Reflective, open to improvement.

Antifragile

Integrates stress and contradiction into higher coherence.

Welcomes challenge, learns rapidly, emotionally grounded.


Growth occurs through exposure to ego stress followed by reflection and integration — analogous to how muscles strengthen after micro-tears.

Psychological theories supporting antifragility


Theory

Key Idea

Relation to Antifragile Ego

Growth Mindset (Dweck, 2006)

Abilities can be developed through effort.

Feedback and failure fuel growth rather than shame.

Self-Compassion (Neff, 2003)

Kindness toward oneself in failure.

Reduces ego defensiveness; enhances learning.

Radical Acceptance (Linehan, 1993)

Accepting reality without judgment.

Allows ego to integrate painful truths without fragmentation.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Identify and restructure distorted beliefs.

Reframes threats as opportunities for calibration.

Ego Development (Loevinger, Cook-Greuter)

Higher ego stages integrate paradox and self-transcendence.

Antifragility reflects mature ego functioning.

Practical techniques to build an antifragile ego

Reframing Criticism

  • View criticism as data rather than attack.
  • Ask: “What kernel of truth might exist here, even if delivery was harsh?”

Controlled Exposure

  • Deliberately engage in situations that challenge ego comfort zones:

    • Public speaking, debate, rejection therapy, or creative critique.
  • Analogous to hormesis in biology — small doses of stress build tolerance.

Journaling and Reflection

  • Reflect after setbacks: What did I learn? What identity assumptions were tested?
  • Use the “observer self” perspective (ACT therapy) — separating you from your ego reactions.

Detachment from Status

  • Practice humility exercises: being wrong publicly, asking naive questions.
  • Internalize that status loss ≠ self-worth loss.

Practice “Self-Antifragility” in Dialogue

  • Seek disconfirming evidence; reward yourself for discovering flaws in reasoning.
  • Train intellectual humility — “strong opinions, weakly held.”

Adopt Feedback Rituals

  • After every major task or meeting:
  • “What went well? What didn’t? What will I do differently next time?”

Antifragility vs. other ego responses


Response Type

Reaction to Challenge

Long-Term Effect

Fragile Ego

Breaks or avoids discomfort.

Stagnation, insecurity.

Defensive Ego

Fights back to protect self-image.

Energy loss, relational conflict.

Stoic Ego (robust)

Endures calmly but unchanged.

Stability without growth.

Antifragile Ego

Adapts, learns, integrates feedback.

Growth, self-mastery, confidence.

Antifragility adds the growth dimension missing from both stoicism and traditional resilience.

Social aspect: power and interpersonal dynamics

As described in The Power Moves article:

  • People with fragile egos often play ego games (one-upmanship, defensiveness, social climbing).
  • Those with antifragile egos don’t depend on constant status reinforcement — they can learn even from subordinates or critics.
  • In relationships, antifragile egos enable authentic communication and reduce reactivity to perceived disrespect.

In leadership, this translates into psychological safety for teams — because the leader’s ego doesn’t punish dissent or mistakes.

Emotional logic


Emotion

Fragile Response

Antifragile Reframe

Shame

“I’m defective.”

“I’ve discovered a growth area.”

Failure

“I lost.”

“I learned data about what doesn’t work.”

Rejection

“I’m unworthy.”

“I’m incompatible here — that’s valuable feedback.”

Criticism

“They attacked me.”

“They revealed how I’m perceived — a new perspective.”

This emotional flexibility is the hallmark of ego antifragility.

Benefits


Domain

Benefits

Personal Growth

Continuous self-improvement through feedback.

Mental Health

Lower anxiety, higher self-esteem stability.

Relationships

Less defensiveness, deeper authenticity.

Leadership

Openness to feedback, trust-building, innovation culture.

Creativity

Fearless experimentation, faster learning from failure.

Resilience to Manipulation

Immunity to shame-based control or validation addiction.

Antifragility in ego produces psychological sovereignty — the self becomes self-correcting and self-reinforcing.

Dangers of a misinterpreted “Antifragile Ego”

  • Pseudo-antifragility: confusing arrogance or indifference with strength. True antifragility isn’t ignoring feedback — it’s learning from it.
  • Narcissistic detachment: pretending not to care to protect self-esteem.
  • Overexposure: seeking excessive criticism or humiliation without integration (ego masochism).
  • Neglecting empathy: growth doesn’t justify emotional coldness.

The antifragile ego thrives on truth, not punishment — feedback must be processed constructively, not destructively.

How to recognize you’re developing an antifragile ego

  • You no longer need to be right — you want to learn what’s true.
  • Criticism stings less and teaches more.
  • You admit mistakes quickly and adjust.
  • You detach your identity from single performances or roles.
  • You can self-criticize without self-loathing.
  • You feel calm in uncertainty because your worth isn’t conditional.

Integration with other psychological models


Related Concept

How It Relates

Antifragility (Taleb)

Conceptual origin — systems that gain from stress.

Self-Actualization (Maslow)

Growth through self-transcendence and authenticity.

Ego Strength (Freud, Erikson)

Ego’s capacity to balance inner and outer demands.

Metacognition (Flavell)

Observing one’s thoughts enhances self-correction.

Post-Traumatic Growth (Tedeschi & Calhoun)

Transformation through adversity parallels antifragile adaptation.

Summary

The antifragile ego is a psychological structure that grows stronger through challenge.

It thrives on truth, learning, and feedback — not validation or avoidance.

Essence

  • Fragile ego: avoids discomfort.
  • Robust ego: resists discomfort.
  • Antifragile ego: transforms discomfort into development.

Mechanisms

  • Self-honesty and self-distancing.
  • Cognitive reframing and identity flexibility.
  • Emotional regulation and reflective practice.

Outcome

  • Inner stability + adaptive evolution = psychological antifragility.

Key takeaways

  • The antifragile ego gains self-knowledge from failure and confidence from transparency.
  • It represents the mature evolution of self-concept: independent, adaptable, and growth-oriented.
  • True antifragility integrates humility, courage, and curiosity.
  • Developing it requires exposure, reflection, and value alignment — not denial or arrogance.


Control situation

Methods

Strategic empathy

Strategic empathy is a concept in communication and negotiation. It involves understanding another person's perspective, needs, and motivations to achieve a common goal. This approach goes beyond just sympathizing with someone; it requires truly comprehending their point of view and using that knowledge to guide your actions or decisions.


Example:

Let's consider a situation in a school setting. Suppose there's a student who consistently disrupts the class. Instead of immediately punishing them, the teacher decides to use strategic empathy. They take time to understand why the student is acting out. Maybe they're bored because the material is too easy for them, or perhaps they're struggling to understand the lessons.


Once the teacher understands the root cause, they can address the issue more effectively. If the student is bored, the teacher might provide more challenging work. If the student is struggling, the teacher could offer extra help or adjust their teaching style to better suit the student's learning needs.


In this way, strategic empathy allows the teacher to create a more positive and productive learning environment.

Confident stillness

Confident stillness is a state of calm and peace that comes from having self-assurance. It's when someone feels secure in their abilities or decisions, so they don't feel the need to constantly act or react. They're comfortable with just being, without feeling restless or anxious.


Example:

Imagine a student who has studied hard for a big test. While others might be nervously flipping through their notes last minute, this student sits quietly, calmly waiting for the test to start. They've prepared well, they trust in their knowledge, and they're not worried about the outcome. This is confident stillness.


Selective vulnerability

In the context of communication and relationships, selective vulnerability refers to the strategic revealing of one's own weaknesses or vulnerabilities at specific moments to create a bond, gain trust, or influence others.


Example:

Consider a politician who is trying to connect with voters. They might share a personal story about struggling with student loans during their college years. This revelation is not accidental; it's a strategic move. By sharing this vulnerability, they are attempting to show that they understand the challenges many voters face. This can make the politician seem more relatable and trustworthy, potentially influencing people to vote for them.


In this case, the politician is using selective vulnerability as a tool to build rapport and influence their audience.

Pattern interruption

Pattern interruption refers to a technique used in various fields, including psychology, communication, and behavior modification, to disrupt or break a person's habitual thought processes, behaviors, or patterns. The goal is often to create a moment of confusion or surprise, allowing for a shift in perspective or the introduction of a new idea. This interruption can be used to break negative thought patterns, overcome mental blocks, or facilitate change.


Example:

Imagine someone is trying to quit smoking, and they have a habit of lighting up a cigarette whenever they feel stressed. A friend, aware of their attempt to quit, might use a pattern interruption by unexpectedly suggesting a spontaneous activity, like going for a quick walk or playing a game. This interrupts the automatic response of reaching for a cigarette when stressed and provides an alternative behavior.


In a broader context, pattern interruption can be applied in various situations, such as breaking negative thought cycles, changing communication dynamics, or helping individuals overcome ingrained habits. It's a versatile concept used in fields like psychology, therapy, coaching, and communication training.


Emotional storytelling

Emotional storytelling is a technique that involves conveying a narrative in a way that evokes strong emotional responses from the audience. It aims to connect with people on a deep, personal level by tapping into universal emotions and experiences. This technique is commonly used in various forms of communication, including marketing, public speaking, and content creation.


Example:

Imagine a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping underprivileged children. Instead of presenting dry statistics about the number of children they've helped, they choose to tell a compelling emotional story.


Practical tips


  1. If you are in customer service, have a mirror somewhere facing the customer. Customers are far less likely to get unreasonably angry when they can see themselves.
  2. If someone only partially answers your question, don't interrupt...wait. You are far more likely to get a complete answer by saying nothing than saying something.
  3. After you state your position in a negotiation, if you are still speaking, you are not speaking in your favor.
  4. If you want to get something from someone, try framing it as though it were an offer instead of a request.
  5. When playing any sport and somebody is on fire, just ask them about their technique. This gets them out of their body and back into their head. What does that accomplish you might ask? Well, it makes them over-think what they’re doing...and mess it up.
  6. When meeting people, try to notice their eye color while you smile at them. You don’t have to mention anything about it, but it’s a good way to make sure that you really look them in the eyes.
  7. As the conventional wisdom goes, a person’s name is the sweetest sound in the world to that person. If you remember a person’s name, you will make that person feel very special indeed.
  8. Chew gum if possible when doing nerve-racking things. It somehow gets your brain to calm down.
  9. If you can get someone to do something simple for you, they are more likely to do something bigger. It’s called gradual commitment or “foot in the door”.
  10. If you work in retail and get angry at customers who are angry at you, you’re just taking the bait. Respond with kindness and the situation will either diffuse, or they’ll go on to act even crazier and make fools out of themselves.
  11. When you are trying to learn something, teach someone about it. It will really cement it into your mind.
  12. If you try to act excited to see people, they will generally respond in kind. Maybe not every time, but as a general rule it holds up pretty well.
  13. Don’t talk about other people behind their backs. In the short run this may be hard when all of your friends are gossiping, but in the long run people will realize that you don’t partake in the gossip and your trust points increase!
  14. People won’t remember what you said. They’ll remember how you made them feel. So don’t worry if you feel like you said something silly, if the overall gist of the conversation was positive, then that is typically how it will be remembered.
  15. Most people’s favorite subject to talk about is themselves. If you don’t know what to talk about, or have awkward silence, just ask them questions.
  16. It’s easy to judge a person’s character by noticing the way they treat people who can’t do anything for them.
  17. When you go on first dates, make them exciting (roller coasters, sky-diving, etc). Your date’s heart will race, adrenaline will flow, and they will indirectly associate the endorphin flood with you. In psychology it’s called the misattribution of arousal.
  18. Emotional expression causes emotion. This means that if you force yourself to smile, your mood will actually improve. Psychologists have even found that people are happier when they are asked to hold chopsticks between their teeth.
  19. If someone is making jokes to the group at your expense, ask them to repeat the joke several times. It seems counter-intuitive, but it will become progressively less funny and nobody will remember it.
  20. When debating, don’t give away your stance first but rather your argument. If you tell people where you stand they will more than likely discard anything you say about the subject because they will already have “understood” your bias (oh, he’s a Republican). If you don’t tell them where you stand, and let it remain a mystery, they will have to piece things together for themselves and really try to understand your argument.
  21. Especially with kids, frame things in a way that always gives them a choice and makes them feel like they are in control. For example, “Do you want to wear your red shirt or your blue shirt?” Either way, they know it’s time to put on a shirt.
  22. Try to replace filler words like “um” with short pauses (to gather your thoughts).
  23. When asking for favors (like cutting in line) try to use the word “because”. Researchers have found that no matter how dumb the reason, the word “because” has the potential to short-circuit people’s brains and make them think it must be okay because there is a reason.
  24. Try to have zero expectations when you are first going into something, it has the potential to prevent disappointment.
  25. Stand up straight. Not only will people see you as more confident, you will actually feel more confident.

Consistency

What is it?

Consistency means different things in different situations; however, the definition of consistency is putting forth a consistent effort day in and day out no matter what you do. There are numerous ways where consistency can be applied.


For example, students need to put forth a consistent effort in their classes. Employees and managers should put forth a consistent effort in their jobs every day. Everyone should be consistent in the effort they put forth in their relationships with their family members, friends, and colleagues.


If you would like to achieve your goals and maintain your relationships, you need to be consistent in the effort you put forth. Even though it is possible to be at your best every day, you should try your best every day. That is the consistency you should strive for. Even though it might be difficult, there are a few ways you can make this easier on yourself.


How to stay consistent?

Consistency is a habit that takes time to develop.

When you come across people who are vigilantly consistent, in many cases, they act as if consistent is just who they are. They rarely go into detail about all the time and focus that it took to become vigilantly consistent. Here’s the truth:


Consistency is NOT a state of mind. It’s a habit that will take you YEARS to develop.

Yes, I said YEARS and setting that realistic expectation will go a long way in helping you not give up on developing the consistency habit when it’s taking longer than you expected.


You’re not going to be vigilantly consistent in every area of your life.

Being vigilantly consistent requires being ALL IN. All in means you are devoting an extreme amount of time to the goal you’re being consistent on… and given that there are only 24 hours in a day, it’s not possible to be vigilantly consistent in ALL areas of your life.


If you’re consistent in exercising 2 hours a day, 6 days a week, you work full time, you have four small children, and you’re married, now saying you want to become vigilantly consistent in meditation 1 hour a day, starting a degree program that requires 20 hours of study time a week, and devote 2 hours a day to write the book you’ve always wanted to write is unrealistic.


Trying to be consistent in all things leads to you being consistent in nothing.


The order in which you develop consistency matters

There is an order of operations to consistency and that order is unique to each individual… which makes it tricky to figure out what your specific consistency order of operations is. At the end of the day, you have to crawl before you walk. In consistency terms, you have to master waking up early FIRST…


For example, before you start scheduling 2 hours of daily writing time from 5–7 am, focus on the waking up early part for 3 or more months BEFORE you add the 2 hours of daily writing time to the mix.


Being consistent requires that your moods don’t dictate your actions

Vigilantly consistent people do what they have to do when they have to do it, regardless of whether they’re in the mood to do those things. Your moods cannot dictate whether or not you take DMA (Daily Massive Action).


If your moods are dictating your decisions about being consistent, you aren’t consistent. If you continually allow your moods to dictate your actions, you will never become consistent.


What you eat impacts your ability to be consistent

When you eat crappy, you feel crappy. What you eat a lot of sugar, carbs, caffeine and other foods that cause insulin spikes, you may have bursts of focus and energy but those bursts are followed by steep crashes in energy. What you eat will determine how consistent you’ll be. Period.


Consistency on the WRONG things keeps you from putting consistency on the RIGHT things

Most people who work on ‘being more consistent’ think they’re currently ‘not consistent.’ Not true at all… Every person is VIGILANTLY CONSISTENT every single day. However, the things you’re currently consistent on may not be the right things to take your life where you want it to go.


You have to make sure that you are being consistent in the areas and on the goals that will create the life you keep saying you want. Otherwise, you still are being consistent- just on the wrong things. Look at your life and assess where you’re currently being consistent. Ask yourself “Is being consistent here getting me closer to where I want to be over there?” If the answer is ‘No’, change where you’re applying your consistency muscles.


Consistency requires obstacles

The TRUE test of consistency is how you’re able to maintain it despite the obstacles that arise. It’s easy to be consistent when there are no challenges to your consistency. When you wake up on time, have no interruptions to your day, and have amazing energy to accomplish all the things, it’s easy to be consistent. Those days are not a true measure of how consistent you are. Your consistency is best assessed when you hit an obstacle, don’t feel like moving forward, and do so anyway.


So… to truly develop vigilant consistency, you have to have obstacles show up in your life AND you have to show yourself that, no matter what obstacle appears, you’re going to choose consistency every time (no matter how inconvenient being consistent is in that moment).


Being consistent is VERY boring

I’m a person who likes excitement. Who am I kidding? I LOVE excitement and this has been one of the most difficult lessons for me to learn. When you become consistent, life gets VERY boring. Day in and day out, you do the same things over and over and over again. After a while, it starts to feel mundane and you start to look for new shiny objects to pique your interest. Don’t do it. The key to your consistency lives in the land of boredom.


James Clear, in his book Atomic Habits, put it best:

“The only way to become excellent is to be endlessly fascinated by doing the same thing over and over. You have to fall in love with boredom.”


It’s hard to be a consistent person with inconsistent friends

To get and stay consistent, you have to develop an environment where consistency is both welcomed and nurtured… and your environment isn’t just where you sleep or the office you work in. Your environment also includes the people you spend time with.


And here’s the deal: If you hang out and spend a lot of time with inconsistent people, it is more likely that you will become inconsistent to match them than they will become vigilantly consistent to match you. Remember: Nobody’s neutral. People either lift you up or pull you down… and your inconsistent friends are a disruption to your consistency.


Bottom line: you’ll have enough obstacles to you getting and staying vigilantly consistent. Your friends don’t need to be an additional obstacle.


Consistency is a long game strategy

There’s no immediate gratification in consistency. Yes, you’ll pat yourself on the back and say “I followed through. I did what I said I was going to do today” and that will make you feel good for five seconds. However, being vigilantly consistent has no immediate payoff. Instead, the benefits of consistency compound over a long period of time.


At the end of the day, being consistent is a long game strategy. If what you want is an immediate sense of victory, consistency will not deliver that to you.


How to improve consistency?

Develop consistent habits

If you are looking for a way to be more consistent in your life, the first thing you need to do is develop more consistent habits. The only way you will be more consistent is if you start from the ground up. There are few ways you can do exactly that. These include: 

  • Be Realistic in Your Goals: You will have a difficult time being consistent if you do not have an idea of what you need to do. Therefore, create easy, simple goals that have objective results that are easy to measure. You could start by defining what consistency means to you. Then, you should come up with smaller steps you have to follow to reach that goal. 
  • Stick to a Schedule: In order to be consistent, you need to know what you have to do every day. Therefore, you should create a schedule for yourself. Whether this is a planner, a calendar, or a list of reminders on your phone, this will help you stay on track. That way, you will figure out what commitments you do and do not have time for.
  • Use Reminders: This is a new habit, so you need to remind yourself what you are doing. Try to place reminders on your belongings, around your home, and throughout your workspace or school. It is easy to forget new commitments and calls, especially when you are trying to change your routine. Put messages in visible locations, so you remind yourself throughout the day. 


Handling mistakes in your routine

No matter how hard you try to be consistent, you are going to make mistakes from time to time. Therefore, try to keep going even if you make a mistake. Even if you are incredibly organized, you are going to slip up from time to time. Therefore, you should plan from mistakes along the way. If you make a mistake, try not to beat yourself up for it. This is something that happens from time to time.


Even if you break a promise, miss a deadline, or have to cancel on somebody, this doesn't necessarily mean you are ruining your consistency. The reality is that external factors can get in the way. Even though it is important to plan for these external factors and try to prevent them from knocking us off track, it will happen from time to time.


Always figure out what you can do next. That way, you can figure out how to improve. Remember that consistency and perfection are not the same things. Nobody is perfect. Be forgiving of yourself; however, do not make a habit of letting things fall through the cracks. 


Increase your willpower

You do not expect to step outside your front door and run a marathon if you haven't done any athletic training. It will take some time for you to build your willpower as well. If you become more consistent, you will increase your willpower, allow you to perform well even when you do not feel like it. Of course, the only way you are going to do that is if you practice.


For example, you should avoid temptation when you can. If you want to be more consistent in what you eat, make sure you have healthy options laying around. This will help you build the willpower to avoid eating junk food. 


Furthermore, you should remind yourself of the long-term benefits of being consistent. Whenever you need a source of inspiration, take a look at your list of goals. This could motivate you to complete everything you have to do during the day even when you do not feel like it. These simple steps can go a long way toward helping you increase your willpower. 


Get plenty of sleep

If you want to be more consistent, you must have the energy to do so. That means you have to get plenty of sleep at night. The average adult needs between seven and eight hours of sleep every evening. People who are still in school require even more.


Give yourself time to change your mindset

Even though you want to see results immediately, it is going to take some time. Changing your thinking is difficult, and it may take a while for you to see results. It can be difficult to uproot your entire life with a bunch of new practices at the same time. Therefore, you should give yourself time to figure out what works best for you.


Also, you should be realistic, but persistent. In general, it takes approximately one month of consistently doing something to make it a habit. Remember to set smaller goes along the way. Try not to tackle too much at once. Small changes will eventually add up.


Furthermore, you will need to set boundaries for your personal relationships and commitments. These boundaries can make it easier for you to keep commitments because you know what to expect from other people.


If you change your thinking, you will become more consistent. Keep this in mind when you are trying to change such a big part of your life.


Take advantage of motivational tools

Humans are not robots, there are going to be days where we do not feel like doing anything. That is why we all need to take advantage of motivational tools. What do you need to do if you need a bit of encouragement to do your work? Even though it can be easy to light our goals slide for a day, there are actions we can take to address this problem. If you feel down, lazy, tired, or in the dumps, there are a few ways you can gather some extra motivation.


Only make promises you can keep

Another important have it you need to develop if you would like to be more consistent is to only make promises you can actually keep. People like to be liked by other people. Therefore, we all have a tendency to say yes when someone asks us for help. Even though it is good to help us other than we can, it is important not to make promises unless we can keep them. If you want to be more consistent in your life, you have to keep the promises you make. On the other hand, it is easy to get overwhelmed, causing certain commitments to fall through the cracks.


Make an effort to reward yourself

If you are trying to become more consistent, make an effort to reward yourself when you do something well. After all, it is not easy to develop a new habit. Try to set time bass goals for yourself. Then, as you hit those goals, reward yourself for doing so. There are plenty of ways you can reward yourself for doing something well.









Methods

Seinfeld Strategy

The Seinfeld Strategy, also known as "Don't Break the Chain," is a method for maintaining focus and consistency in pursuing long-term goals. Coined after comedian Jerry Seinfeld, this strategy involves visually tracking daily progress on a calendar. The primary objective is to undertake a specific activity every day, marking each completed day with a satisfying visual cue, such as a prominent 'X' on the calendar. The technique relies on the motivational power of continuity - as the chain of marked days grows longer, the individual's commitment intensifies, making it progressively harder to break the chain.


The Seinfeld Strategy is remarkably versatile, making it suitable for a diverse range of individuals seeking to improve their productivity and maintain consistency in pursuing their goals. It is especially beneficial for:

  • Students striving to establish effective study habits
  • Professionals aiming to enhance work performance and time management
  • Individuals committed to personal development and self-improvement
  • Creatives, including writers, artists, and musicians, pursuing regular practice and output
  • Individuals undertaking health and wellness goals, such as exercise, meditation, or dietary changes


Pros

The Seinfeld Strategy is acclaimed for its numerous benefits, including:

  1. Enhanced Consistency: The strategy fosters a daily habit-forming process, ensuring consistent progress toward goals.
  2. Motivational Momentum: The visual representation of the unbroken chain stimulates motivation and a sense of achievement, reinforcing the commitment to the task.
  3. Simplicity and Flexibility: Its straightforward approach and adaptability across different tasks make it accessible and applicable to a wide range of pursuits.

Cons

While the Seinfeld Strategy provides substantial advantages, it is essential to consider potential drawbacks, such as:

  1. Rigidity: The method's focus on daily activities might result in undue pressure, leading to burnout or demotivation if strict adherence becomes burdensome.
  2. Risk of Sabotage: Unavoidable interruptions or setbacks may jeopardize the continuity of the chain, potentially demoralizing individuals who may perceive it as a failure.


Steps

  1. Identify the Target Habit or Activity
  2. Establish a Visual Tracking System
  3. Set Daily Commitments
  4. Initiate the Chain
  5. Cultivate Discipline and Resilience
  6. Reflect on Progress and Adapt
  7. Reap the Fruits of Consistency

Decision making

What it is?

Decision-making skill is the ability to choose between different options by considering the possible outcomes. It involves critical thinking, analyzing information, understanding the consequences, and making a choice that best suits your goals or the needs of a situation. Good decision-makers also learn from past choices to improve future decisions.

Decision-making process

The decision-making process is a series of steps you take to choose the best action from several options. It's how you figure out what to do in different situations, especially when the outcome matters a lot.

Step 1: Identify the decision that needs to be made

When you're identifying the decision, ask yourself a few questions: 

  • What is the problem that needs to be solved?
  • What is the goal you plan to achieve by implementing this decision?
  • How will you measure success?

These questions are all common goal setting techniques that will ultimately help you come up with possible solutions. When the problem is clearly defined, you then have more information to come up with the best decision to solve the problem.

Step 2: Gather relevant information

Collecting relevant information is vital for informed decision-making. Does your team have historical data on this issue, or has anyone previously tried to solve it? Seek information beyond your team or company; consider market research, consulting experts, or discussing with experienced peers from other companies. This broadens the range of potential solutions.

Step 3: Identify alternative solutions

Explore multiple solutions for the issue, considering varied stakeholder needs. For instance, a design team and a development team may require different features in a work management tool; thus, opting for a single solution immediately may be unwise.

Step 4: Weigh the evidence

This is when you take all of the different solutions you’ve come up with and analyze how they would address your initial problem. Your team begins identifying the pros and cons of each option, and eliminating alternatives from those choices.

There are a few common ways your team can analyze and weigh the evidence of options:

  • Pros and cons list
  • SWOT analysis
  • Decision matrix

Step 5: Choose among the alternatives

Make your final decision by evaluating the impact on stakeholders and considering a blend of alternatives. Think creatively and don't restrict yourself to obvious choices; combine options for greater benefits.

Step 6: Take action

Once the final decision maker gives the green light, it's time to put the solution into action. Take the time to create an implementation plan so that your team is on the same page for next steps. Then it’s time to put your plan into action and monitor progress to determine whether or not this decision was a good one. 

Step 7: Review your decision and its impact (both good and bad)

Once you’ve made a decision, you can monitor the success metrics you outlined in step 1. This is how you determine whether or not this solution meets your team's criteria of success.

Here are a few questions to consider when reviewing your decision:

  • Did it solve the problem your team identified in step 1? 
  • Did this decision impact your team in a positive or negative way?
  • Which stakeholders benefited from this decision? Which stakeholders were impacted negatively?

If this solution was not the best alternative, your team might benefit from using an iterative form of project management. This enables your team to quickly adapt to changes, and make the best decisions with the resources they have. 

Types

Rational decision making models
